editorialDecl.p: New English translation produced by the Falsafa project (Thothica) using an in-house agentic AI translation system, rendered from the Perseus source edition and reviewed by the project. Contributed to provide a translation for a work that previously had no English translation in the corpus.

div.p: Of brother battle-lines, and reigns contested in alternation through unholy hatreds, and guilty Thebes laid bare, a Pierian fire falls on my mind: from where do you bid me begin, you goddesses? Shall I sing the origins of that dread race, the Sidonian rape and the inexorable pact of Agenor's law, and Cadmus searching the seas? Long is the chain that stretches back, if I should trace the trembling farmer of buried war, who sowed unspeakable battles in his furrows, and follow it deep — by what song Amphion bade the Tyrian mountains draw near to make his walls, whence came Bacchus's heavy wrath against his kindred city, what was the work of cruel Juno, against whom unhappy Athamas took up his bow, why the mother, doomed to fall with her companion Palaemon, did not dread the vast Ionian sea; and so for now I will let the griefs and the prosperous days of Cadmus pass: let the boundary of my song be the troubled house of Oedipus, since I would not yet dare to breathe of Italian standards, of triumphs in the North, of the Rhine twice brought beneath the yoke, the Danube twice subdued by law, and the Dacians hurled down from their sworn ridge, or the wars of Jove defended first in years scarcely past boyhood, and you, O glory added to the Latin name, whom Rome, as you take up early your father's fresh beginnings, desires to be forever her own — though every narrower boundary should drive the stars, and the bright tract of heaven sue for you, the region free of the Pleiades, of the North Wind, and of cleaving lightning, though the curber of the fire-footed horses should himself press upon your hair his radiant bow, or great Jupiter yield to you an equal share of the pole — remain content with the reins of men, master of waves and earth, and let the stars be your gift. A time will come when, stronger in Pierian frenzy, I shall sing your deeds: now I tune my lyre, content to tell the Aonian arms, the scepter ruinous to two tyrants, the rage that knew no measure even after death, the rebellious flames in the strife of the pyre, the funerals of kings deprived of tombs, and cities emptied by reciprocal slaughter, when blue Dirce blushed with Lernaean blood and Thetis shuddered as Ismenos, used to grazing his parched banks, came down to her with a mighty heap of corpses. Which of the heroes, Clio, will you give me first? Tydeus, boundless in his rage? Or the prophet, suddenly engulfed and crowned with laurel? Wild Hippomedon also presses on, driving before him a river choked with the enemy slain; and there are the wars of the bold Arcadian, to be wept for, and Capaneus, who must be sung with another dread.

Now, having searched out his guilty eyes with deserving hand, Oedipus had plunged his condemned shame in everlasting night and dragged out his life beneath a lingering death; yet as he hid himself in the dark, in the recess of his deepest seat, guarding a household unseen by heaven and its rays, still around him on tireless wings flew the cruel daylight of his mind, and in his breast the Furies of his crimes. Then he displays his empty sockets, that raw and pitiable punishment of life, to heaven, and with bloodied hands beats the hollow ground and prays in this savage voice: 'You gods who rule guilty souls and Tartarus narrow with its torments, and you, Styx, livid in your shadowy depth, whom I behold, and Tisiphone, so often summoned at my call, favor me; smile upon my perverse prayers. If I have earned anything well — if, when I fell from my mother, you cherished me in your lap and steadied my feet pierced by the wound; if I sought the Cirrhaean pools that lie between the twin-horned ridge, when I might have lived content with a false Polybus; if in the narrow strait of three-forked Phocis I tangled with the aged king and cut through the cries of the screaming old man while I searched for my father; if, by your prompting, I cunningly unraveled the riddling ambiguities of the unjust Sphinx; if I gladly entered upon sweet madness and the lamentable marriage of my mother, and again and again endured that unspeakable night, and fathered children for you — as you yourself know — and then, greedy for punishment, with my own self-rending fingers fell upon my eyes and left them in my wretched mother: hear me, if what I pray is fitting, and such as you yourself might prompt a madman. The sons I begot on whatever bed, left fatherless and stripped of his eyes and crown, they did not try to guide, nor to soften my grief with words; nay, look — proud, and (the pity of it!) already kings over my living burial, they mock my darkness and loathe their father's groans. Am I death-bringing even to these? And does the idle father of the gods look on at all this? You at least, due avenger, come here, and begin the punishment of all my descendants. Set on your brow the diadem that I, soaked in gore, tore off with bloodied nails, and, urged by a father's prayers, go between the brothers, let the bonds of kinship be cleft apart by the sword. Grant, queen of the Tartarean pit, the unspeakable thing I long to have seen, and the minds of the young men will not be slow to follow; only come worthy of yourself — you will know them for my offspring.'

As he spoke thus, the cruel goddess turned her stern face toward him. She chanced to be sitting beside the unlovely Cocytus, and had loosed the snakes from her head to let them lap the sulphurous waters; at once, swifter than the fire of Jove or falling stars, she leapt up from the gloomy banks: the empty crowd withdraws and dreads to meet its mistress; she, through the shadows and the fields dim with the swarm of souls, seeks the irreversible threshold of the Taenarian gate. Daylight felt her coming; Night, facing her in a pitch-black cloud, threw her shining horses into confusion; far off, towering Atlas shuddered and let the sky slip on his faltering neck. At once, rising again from the valley of Malea, she seizes the familiar road to Thebes: for no other ways does she travel, going and returning, more swiftly, nor does she prefer her kindred Tartarus. A hundred horned serpents standing upright shadowed her face, the menacing throng of her dread head; deep within sat an iron light in her eyes, such as the toil of Phoebe reddens through the clouds by Thessalian craft; her skin, steeped in venom, is stretched taut and swells with corruption; a fiery breath comes from her black mouth, by which long thirst and sickness and hunger and a single death come upon whole peoples; on her back stiffens a horrid robe, and the dark-blue knots meet again across her breast: Atropos and Proserpina herself renew this attire. Then in her wrath she shakes both hands: this one flashes with the fire of the pyre, that one lashes the air with a living water-snake.

When she stood where Cithaeron rises sheerest from its crag to meet the sky, with her green hair she doubled her wild hissing — a signal to the lands, by which all the shores of the Achaean sea and the realms of Pelops echoed far and wide: mid-heaven's Parnassus heard it, and rugged Eurotas, and the crash drove wavering Oeta upon its ridge to one side, and the Isthmus scarcely held back its twin seas. The mother herself snatched away her son Palaemon as he wandered on his curving dolphin, and pressed him to her breast.

And when, headlong, she first halted on the Cadmean summit and infected the household with her accustomed cloud, straightway in the brothers' hearts rose troubled passions, and an ancestral fury entered their minds, and envy sick at another's joy, and fear, the parent of hatred; then the savage love of ruling, the alternations broken, and ambition impatient of a second turn, and the sweetness of standing alone at the summit, and discord, the companion of shared kingdoms. So when the farmer seeks to yoke chosen bullocks from the wild herds together beneath the plow, they, indignant — bulls whose lofty necks have not yet sunk into their knotted shoulders under much plowing — pull in opposite directions, slacken the bonds with equal strength, and confound the furrows with a wandering line: not otherwise does headlong discord goad on the untamed brothers. It was agreed to exchange their ruler by exile under the law of alternate years; thus by a malignant rule they bid fortune pass between them, so that the one holding the scepter should always be pressed, by a hurried pact, by a new heir. This was the brothers' love, this the only delay to battle, nor would it endure into the second king's reign. Not yet did golden paneled ceilings gleam thick with metal, nor halls upheld high on Grecian marble shine, spacious enough to spread out crowds of clients; no spears watched over the uneasy sleep of kings, no guards groaned at their alternating shifts of arms, no care to set gems afloat in unmixed wine, or defile gold with food: but naked power armed the brothers; the fight is over a beggar kingdom. And while it is disputed which of them should turn over the squalid acres of cramped Dirce, or, no higher on the throne of a Tyrian exile, exult, right and law and good have perished, and all shame of life and death. To what end do you stretch your wrath, ah, wretched ones? What if the boundaries of either pole were sought by such great crime — the bounds that the Sun, sent forth from the Eastern gate, beholds, and that he beholds again sinking toward the Iberian harbor, and whatever lands he touches afar with his slanting beam, remote, whether cold under the North Wind or warm and drenched with the fire of the South? Not if the wealth of Phrygia and of Tyre were brought together under one rule. The dreadful place and the accursed citadels sufficed for their hatred, and to have sat, bought with monstrous madness, in the seat of Oedipus.

Now the honor, deferred by lot, had passed from Polynices. What, then, was that day to you, cruel one — what day was it, when alone in the empty hall you looked round and saw all the right was yours, and all men lesser than you, and nowhere a head that stood your equal? Already the murmurs of the Echionian people creep abroad, and the silent crowd sets itself against its prince, and (as is the way of peoples) the one to come is loved. And someone, whose mind was bent to wound the great with humble poison, and who would never bear willingly the rulers set on his neck, said: 'Has harsh fate brought this turn upon Ogygian affairs, so often to change our dreaded masters and bend our doubting necks beneath an alternating yoke? Divided, they twist the destinies of peoples and with their hands have made fortune fickle. Shall I always in turn be made to serve exiles? On you, highest of the gods and sower of the lands, did it settle to put this purpose into the partners? Or is it from this that the old omen for Thebes extends, ever since Cadmus, an exile, bidden to seek through Carpathian waters the alluring weight of the Sidonian bullock — and sought in vain — found a kingdom across the Hyantean fields, and from the gaping of the teeming earth sent down the augury of fraternal battle-lines to his late descendants?' You see how, with menacing brow, power risen up, fiercer now its consort is removed, threatens raised on high; what threats it carries on its face, with what pride it crushes all! Will this one ever be a private man? Yet that other, to a suppliant, was gentle and kind in speech and more patient of what is fair. What wonder? He was not alone. We, a cheap rabble, our hands ready for every chance, prepared for whatever master, just as on this side the cold North Wind, on that the cloud-bringing East drag the sails, and the fortune of the ship between them wavers — alas, the harsh lot held suspended in uncertain fear, to be endured by no people! — this one commands, that one threatens.'

But at Jove's command, above the halls of the swift heaven, in the inner pole, a chosen company had gathered to the council of the gods. From there all things lie close at hand — the homes of the first dawn and the setting sun, and all that is spread beneath every land and sea by day. The lofty god himself enters among the gods, shaking all things yet with a calm face, and takes his place on a star-bright throne: nor at once did the heaven-dwellers dare, until the father himself with a tranquil hand bade them have leave to sit. Soon the throng of wandering demigods, and the Rivers kindred to the highest clouds, and the Winds, keeping their murmurs pressed down in fear, fill the golden halls; the vaults tremble, mingled with the majesty of the gods; the rooftops shine with a greater calm, and the doorposts flower with a secret light. After quiet was commanded and the awe-struck world fell silent, he begins from on high — a grave and unalterable weight attends the holy words, and the fates follow his voice: 'I complain of the crimes of earth and the mind of mortals, insatiable to the Furies: to what point shall I be wearied out in punishing the guilty? It tires me to rage with the flashing thunderbolt; long since the laboring arms of the Cyclopes grow faint, and the fires fail on the Aeolian anvils. And so I had borne the horses of the Sun let loose under a false driver, and the heaven scorched by the wandering wheels, and the world laid waste by Phaethon's embers — nothing was gained; nor that you, brother, gave the sea to go far through the forbidden with your strong trident. Now I come down to punish two houses, whose blood I myself begot. One splits off to Perseus's Argos, the other flows from its source to Aonian Thebes. The same mind set upon all remains: who could be ignorant of the funerals of Cadmus, and how the host of Eumenides, so often roused from their lowest seats, has made war — the wicked joys of mothers, the wild wanderings of the groves, and the crimes of the gods that must not be told? Scarce in a day's space, scarce in a fled night could I number their ways and their unhallowed race. Nay, even to climb his father's chamber this impious heir desired, and to defile the womb of his guiltless mother, turned back — a monstrous thing! — to his own beginnings. Yet he paid the gods eternal atonement and cast away the day, and no longer feeds on our upper air; but his sons — a deed without precedent! — trampled his fallen eyes. Now, now you have your prayers fulfilled, dreadful old man! Your darkness has earned, has earned the right to hope for Jove as avenger. New arms I shall hurl upon the guilty realms, and tear up by the root the whole deadly stock. Let the seeds of war be for me Adrastus the father-in-law, and the marriages joined under sinister gods. This race too it is decreed to assail with punishments; for not from my secret heart have treacherous Tantalus and the outrage of the cruel banquet perished.'

So the almighty father; but she, wounded by his words, turning over in her inflamed heart an unforeseen grief, Juno replies thus: 'Do you bid me, O most just of the gods, do you bid me make war? You know how I have always favored the citadels of the Cyclopes and the scepter of great Phoroneus, famed in renown, with men and with wealth, though there, shameless, you put to death by sleep and slaughter the guardian of the Pharian heifer, and entered, turned to gold, the walled towers. Your lying beds I pardon: it is that city I hate. Whose face you openly own when you approach, where you wield the thunder, the sign of our great bed, and brandish my own lightnings. Let Thebes pay for its deeds: why do you choose Argos for your enemy? Nay, come — if the discord of the sacred chamber is so great, raze with arms both Samos and ancient Mycenae, overthrow Sparta to the ground. Why anywhere on a festal day does the altar of your wife grow warm with blood, why with a heap of Eastern incense does it glow rejoicing? Better do Mareotic Coptos and the mourning streams of the Nile of Acrisius smoke with vows to you. But if peoples atone for the ancient crimes of their founders, and this late sentence comes to the aid of your concerns — to review the old age of the world, at what time at last it is enough to abolish the frenzies of the earth and to amend the ages back — then long since begin from those abodes, where the wave-wandering Alpheus glides past, seeking far away his Sicilian love. Here the Arcadians — and there is no shame in it — have set your shrines in unholy places; there the Martial chariot of Oenomaus, and a herd more fit to be stabled under Getic Haemus, where even now the broken faces of the unburied suitors stiffen among the scattered remains. Yet here the honor of a temple is welcome to you; you favor guilty Ida and Crete, which lies of your ghost. As for me standing on Tantalus's lands — what envy is this at last? Turn aside the tumults of war and have pity on your own race. Wide are the impious realms you have, which will better bear guilty sons-in-law.'

Juno had ended, mingling reproaches with her prayers. But he, not grieved by her words, though they were harsh in their stirring, made this reply: 'Indeed I did not think you would bear with a kindly mind whatever I should resolve concerning your Argos, however justly, nor, if the chance were given, does it escape me that you would say much in defense of Thebes, and that Dione would dare to speak. But reverence for our authority forbids it. For by the dread waters, the Stygian streams of my brother, I swear — a word abiding and beyond recall — nothing shall be that can bend me from my decree! Therefore go, swift on your wings; go before the winds that bear you, offspring of Cyllene, gliding through the clear air and into the shadowy realms, and say to my uncle: let aged Laius raise himself to the upper airs — Laius, whom, slain by his son's wound, the farther bank of deep Lethe has not yet received by the law of Erebus; let him bear my commands to his dread grandson: his brother, relying on exile and swollen with the Argive welcome that he himself willingly seeks, let the impious one bar far from his hall, denying him the alternate honor of the kingdom. Hence will come the causes of wrath; the rest I shall lead on in a fixed order.'

The son of Atlas obeys his father's words, and then swiftly binds to his feet the winged sandals, shrouds his hair, and tempers the stars with his hat. Then he set in his right hand the wand by which he was used to drive away or to summon again sweet sleep, by which to enter black Tartarus and to give life to the bloodless shades; he leapt down, and as the thin air caught him, he shivered. Without delay, sublime, in headlong flight he cuts through the void and marks the clouds with a vast arc.

Meanwhile the son of Oedipus, long a wandering exile from his native shores, ranges by stealth through the deserts of Aonia, and even now in his heart he conceives the kingdom ill owed to him, and groans that the long year stands still while its signs delay. One care, returning by day and by night, holds the man: whether he might ever see his brother step down, humbled, from the throne, while he himself takes possession of Thebes and its wealth; for this light he would bargain his life. Now he complains of the slow losses of his exile, but soon he lifts up a leader's pride, and proud, with his brother now cast down, he thinks himself enthroned: anxious hope draws out his mind and consumes his joys in long desire. He is then resolved to make the journey, undaunted, to the Inachian cities and the fields of Danaus and Mycenae, dark with the broken sun, whether the Fury leads him on before, or it was the chance of the road, or unmoved Atropos called him this way. He leaves the caverns howled over by the Ogygian frenzies and the hills fattened with Bacchic blood, then passes the tract where Cithaeron, gently sitting, stretches out into the plain and slopes its weary mountain to the sea; from there, hanging by a narrow path on the cliffs, he leaves behind the infamous rocks of Sciron and the Scyllaean lands ruled by the purple-haired old man, and gentle Corinth, and in the midst of the plains hears the two shores.

And now Titanis, rising over the borders of the spent Sun-god, borne up high over a silent world, had thinned the cold air with her dew-bearing pair of horses: now flocks and birds fall silent, now Sleep has crept upon greedy cares and nods, leaning down from the sky, bringing the welcome forgetfulness of life's labor. But the clouds gave no promise that the gleam would return to the crimson sky, nor, as the shadows thinned, did the long twilight shine with Phoebus thrown back: denser from the earth, and pierced by no flame, black night weaves a curtain beneath the poles. Now the barriers of frozen Aeolia, struck, resound, and the storm to come threatens with hoarse voice; the winds, roaring crosswise, clash, and tear the firmament from its uprooted hinge, while each seizes the sky for himself; but most of all the South Wind heaps up the night, twisting its dark folds, and pours down rains, which rough Boreas with his dry maw freezes hard beforehand; nor any less do the sudden lightnings quiver, and the aether, rubbed, is split by a sudden flame. Now Nemea, now the high heads of Arcadia, bordering the Taenarian groves, run wet; in a great column rushes down Inachus, and Erasmus rising into its icy floods. Streams once dusty and dried-up no delays held back with banks, and Lerna was poured back to its depths in pools and foamed with its ancient venom. Every grove is broken; the gales tear the ancient arms of the forests, and the summer haunts of shady Lycaeus, beheld by no suns through all the ages, lay open. But he, now marveling at the rocks that fled from the cracked ridges, now fearing in his ear the cloud-born torrents from the mountains, and the homes of shepherds and of flocks snatched up everywhere by the mad whirlwind, no less frantic and uncertain of his way, through the black silences drains his vast journey; fear strikes him on every side, and on every side his brother. And as a sailor caught on the wintry sea, to whom neither the sluggish Wain nor the Moon with a friendly star shows the way, stands helpless of reason amid the tumult of sky and sea, and now, now expects either the rocks sunk in the malignant shallows, or that the foaming crags should rush upon the upreared prow with their sharp peak: so the Cadmean hero, threading the dark of the woods, hastens, shaking with his vast shield-boss the fearful dens of the beasts, and breaking the thickets with his bent chest; the grim force of fear gives spurs to his spirit, until from the Inachian dwellings, the gloom conquered, the Larissaean height flashed out, pouring its light upon the sloping walls. Roused by it with all hope, he flies forth, keeping on his left the Junonian temples of lofty Prosymna, on the other side the black pools of the Lernaean shallows, marked by the heat of Hercules; and at last he is borne through the unbarred gates, and straightway sees the royal vestibule. Here he flings down his limbs, stiff with rain and wind, and leaning on the doorposts of the unknown hall, invites scant sleep to his hard couch.

There ruled the people Adrastus, a king in tranquil times, from the middle limit of life inclining toward old age, rich in ancestors and tracing his descent from Jove on both sides of his blood. He lacked the better sex, but flourished in female offspring, supported by the twin pledge of his daughters. To him Phoebus had foretold — a deadly thing to tell, though afterward the faith was made clear — with fate as guide, that sons-in-law would come, a bristling boar and a tawny lion; this neither the father himself, nor Amphiaraus, learned in things to come, can read, for Apollo the author forbids it; only, settled in his heart, the care grows sick in the parent. But behold, leaving ancient Calydon by fate, Olenian Tydeus — the horror, conscious of his brother's blood, drives him on — under the same drowsy night treads the same wild places, and complaining of the like winds and rains, bearing on his back the ice melted and his face and hair streaming with the storm-clouds, enters under one roof, of which the earlier guest, sprawled on the cold ground, held the better part. Here indeed fortune brought to both a bloody madness: they would not suffer their fellow to share the night under the same shelter; a little while, in alternating words and threats, they hesitate; soon, when the bandied speeches had swollen their wrath enough, then indeed each, drawn up, bared his shoulders and provoked the contest hand to hand. That one was taller in stride, with long limbs, and at the same time whole in his years; but in strength his spirit bears Tydeus no lower, and the greater valor, poured through all his frame, reigned in his small body. Now they redouble their crowding blows about the face and the hollow temples, straining, like a hail of weapons or the storm of Riphaean hail, and with bent knee they batter the unguarded flanks. Not otherwise than when his own festivals return for the Pisaean Thunderer, and the dust burns with the raw sweat of men; and on this side the rivalry of the arena rouses the tender youths, and the shut-out mothers await the prizes: so, eager with hatred and kindled by no desire of praise, they rush together, and the hooked hand searches out the deepest of the face and enters, the eyes giving way, deep within. And perhaps — for so their wrath was carrying them — they would have bared the swords girt at their sides, and better, mourned by your brother, slain by hostile arms, you would have lain, young man of Thebes, had not the king, marveling at the strange clamor and the groans hissing from the deep breast amid the shadows of night, moved his steps — the king whose old age, sober with great cares, hung on a sleep already poorer. And as he came forward through the lofty halls with many lights, the bars drawn back at the facing threshold, he sees a sight terrible to tell: faces torn, and cheeks foul with a bloody shower: 'What is the cause of your fury, foreign youths — for none of my own citizens would dare raise his hands to such a deed — what implacable passion is this to drive out with hatred the tranquil silences of the night? Is the day so cramped, and so grievous, that you cannot for a little suffer peace in your mind and sleep? But declare at last: whence are you sprung, where do you bear your journey, what is your quarrel? For you no humble men, such great wrath teaches, and the great signs of a proud lineage shine through the spilled blood.'

Scarcely had he spoken, when, with mingled outcry, glaring sidelong, they begin together: 'O king, gentlest of the Achaeans, what need of words? Do you yourself behold these faces streaming with blood?' These things, here and there, with the confused sounds of their bitter voices, they jumbled out: then, beginning in order, Tydeus went on: 'Desiring solace for my mournful misfortune, I left the wealth of monster-breeding Calydon and the Acheloian fields. Lo, this vast night covers me in your borders; who is this who forbade me to keep the sky off by a roof? Or is it because I first chanced to set my steps toward this threshold? They tell us the two-formed Centaurs share a stable together, and the Cyclopes in Aetna are settled as one; and even on savage monsters laws are imposed, and a right of their own: shall we not share the lodgings of the earth? — But why do I? Either today, whoever you are, you will go off rejoicing in your spoils, or you will find me — if my blood, worn out, is not numbed by a sudden grief — sprung from the stock of great Oeneus, and not degenerate from my father Mars.' 'Nor do we lack in spirit or in stock' — he answers in turn; but his mind, conscious of its fate, hesitates to declare his father. Then gentle Adrastus: 'Nay, come, and laying aside the threats that the night and the sudden chance, or your valor or your wrath, advised, come beneath my roof; now let your right hands join together as pledges of your hearts. Not in vain is this done, nor with the gods absent; perhaps a love to come has sent these wraths before it, so that the remembering may be sweet.' Nor in vain did the old man speak his words, since they say that by this faith, joined through their wounds, those two went on — as great as it shared its end with bold Pirithous and Theseus, or as Orestes, his mind empty, escaped the raging Megaera with Pylades set against her. Then too, while the king with his words soothed their harsh hearts, now grown easy — as the seas, contested by the winds, subside, and yet a surviving breeze lingers long, dying upon the slackened sails — they suffered themselves, and went beneath the household roof.

Here first he has leisure to survey with his eyes the dress of the men and their great weapons: on the back of this one he sees an empty lion bristling, its mane unkempt on either side, in the likeness of that one which through the Teumesian valley the son of Amphitryon, broken in his youthful years, had clothed himself in before the battle of the Cleonaean monster; on the other side, dreadful with bristles and curving tusk, the spoils struggle to wind around Tydeus's broad shoulders, the glory of Calydon. The old man stands fixed, amazed at the great omen, recognizing the divine oracles of Phoebus and the warnings given from the speaking caverns; in his gaze he holds his cold lips, and a glad shudder ran through his limbs; he felt that they were brought by a manifest power to be present — those whom Apollo the augur, in tangled riddles, had declared would be portended as his sons-in-law, with the deceiving face of beasts. Then thus, stretching his palms to the stars: 'Night, you who, embracing the labors of earth and sky, send the fiery stars across in their many-wandering glide, indulgent to renew the spirit, until the next Titan pours over the weary the nimble risings for living things, you of your own accord bring me the faith I sought through tangled wanderings, kindly one, and uncover the beginnings of an ancient fate: stand by my work and confirm your omens. Forever honored, when the years' orbits are measured out, this house will worship you; for you, goddess, dark herds with chosen necks shall be sacrificed, and the Vulcanian fire, drenched with new milk, shall consume the lustral entrails. Hail, ancient faith of the tripods and the obscure recesses! I have caught you, Fortune, and the gods!' So he spoke, and binding both by their hands, he goes forward to the dwellings of the inner hall. The fires on the altars still kept their slumbering ash and the offerings of the warm rite; he bids the hearths be kindled and the fresh feast restored; the servants, obedient to his words, hasten eagerly; the palace, struck, clamors with varied tumult: some cover with purple the slender couches that sound with gold, and lay the high tapestries upon them; others smooth with their hands the polished tables and set them in order. But others, undertaking to conquer the darkness and the murky night, stretch out the cords on the gilded lamps. For some the task is to roast on inserted iron the bloodless flesh of the slaughtered beasts; for some, to heap in baskets the corn ground on the stone; Adrastus rejoices that his house seethes with service. And now he himself shone in proud coverings, propped on an ivory throne. In another part the young men, their wounds dried with water, recline, and at the same time look on the faces marred with marks, and in turn forgive each other. Then the aged king bids Acaste — she who was the nurse of his daughters, and the same their most faithful guardian, chosen to conceal the holy shame owed to chaste Venus — be summoned, and murmurs into her silent ear.

No delay to his commands, when straightway both the maidens came forth from the secret chamber: a wondrous sight, they bear faces equal to those of arms-clashing Pallas and quivered Diana, only with less terror; then the new sight of men seemed to them a thing for modesty: equally pallor and blush drained their crimson cheeks, and their shy eyes returned to their holy father, after, when in the order of the meal hunger was conquered, the son of Iasus by custom asked his servants for a bowl finished with figures and gleaming with gold, from which Danaus and the elder Phoroneus were used to pour libation to the gods; this holds carved images of deeds: a golden winged one holds the snake-haired Gorgon with neck cut off, and now, now into the wandering airs — so it seemed — he leaps; she barely moves her heavy eyes and languishing face, and grows pale even in the living gold. On this side the Phrygian hunter is lifted up on tawny wings, Gargara sinks as he rises and Troy recedes, his companions stand mournful, and the dogs in vain weary their sounding mouths, and seek the shadow and bark at the clouds. This bowl, pouring out the foaming wine, he uses to invoke in order all the heaven-dwellers, Phoebus before the rest; Phoebus to the altar he summons with the praise of all his companions and servants, his hand bound with chaste foliage, he for whom is a festal day, and the fires, refreshed with abundant incense, shine on the vaporing altars. 'Perhaps, young men, you may ask in your minds what these rites are, and for what causes we beseech the special honor of Phoebus,' the king says: 'no ignorant religion has prompted it; the Argive people, once tried by great disasters, make this offering; turn your minds to me, and I will unfold it. After the god struck down the winding coils of the dark-blue monster, the earth-born Python, who clasped Delphi in seven black circles and bore on his scales the trees of ages, while, sprawled at the Castalian springs with his three-forked mouth, he gaped, thirsting for nourishment from his black venom — the god struck him, his weapons spent in countless wounds, and stretched him out, scarcely at last unrolled, over a hundred acres of the Cirrhaean field; then, seeking new atonements for the slaughter, he reached the not-wealthy dwelling of our Crotopus, whose daughter, in the first years just entering youth, of wondrous beauty, kept the dutiful household undefiled by any bed — happy, had she never joined to Phoebus a Delian theft and a hidden love! For when, having yielded to the god at the wave of the Nemean river, Cynthia with full face resumed her tenth orbit, the bride brought forth a starry grandson for Latona; and, fearing punishment — for that father would not have granted pardon to a forced bridal — she chooses the pathless fields, and stealthily entrusts her son among the fenced sheepfolds to a mountain-wandering keeper of the flock to be reared. No cradle worthy of so great a stock, my boy, did the grass give you for your couch, and a house woven of oaken wicker; your limbs grow warm under the bark of the strawberry-tree's rind, and the hollow reed-pipe coaxes light sleep, and the ground is shared with the flock. But the fates did not grant him even that hearth: for, cast carelessly on the green turf of the earth and drawing the open sky with gaping mouth, the dread madness of dogs, feeding with bloody bite, tore him apart. And when as a messenger this reaches the mother's astonished ears, from her mind were driven father and shame and fear: of her own accord, mad with savage lamentations, she fills the house, and bearing her breast bare of its covering runs to her father confessing all; nor is he moved, and bids her — unspeakable! — die by a black death, though she herself desired it. Too late mindful of the marriage, Phoebus, you prepare for her mournful death a solace, a monster conceived in deep Acheron in the chambers of the Eumenides, which had a maiden's face and breast; an everlasting hissing rises from its crown, and a snake parts its iron-gray forehead. This dire plague then, squalid in its nocturnal pace, would glide into the chambers, and snatch souls fresh from the stock from their nurses' laps, and devour them with bloody bite, and grow fat upon a father's grief. But Coroebus, outstanding in arms and in spirit, did not bear it, and of his own accord offered himself among the chosen youths, who, first in strength, were ready, careless of their lives, to extend their fame; she was going, ravaging the new homes, at the fork of the gates — two little bodies hang at her side, and now her hooked hand clings to their vitals, and her iron nails grow warm beneath the tender heart — the youth, a crowd of men thronging on every flank, meets her, and buried his huge sword beneath her hard breast, and, searching out with his flashing blade the deepest hiding-places of her life, at last gives her own monster back to be held by deep Jove. It is a joy to go and look close on the eyes livid in death, and on the unspeakable discharge of her belly, and her breast squalid with thick gore, where our souls had perished. The Inachian youth stand amazed, and even after their tears their great joys still are pale. Some, with hard logs — a vain solace for grief — trample her lifeless limbs, and crush rough millstones into her cheeks: their power cannot fill their wrath, and you, unfed birds flying with nocturnal hissing around her, fled, and the mad force of dogs and the dry mouths of trembling wolves, men say, gaped after her. Fiercer against the wretched, robbed of the avenging fate, the Delian rises up, and sitting in the high shadow of twin-peaked Parnassus, with his cruel bow, unjust, hurls his pestilent arms, and sets the plains and the high dwellings of the Cyclopes ablaze under a thrown-on cloak of mists. The sweet souls slip away; Death with his sword reaps the threads of the Sisters, and holding the captured city carries it in his hands. To the leader asking what was the cause, what sinister fire from the sky reigned, and why Sirius held the whole year in its sway, the same author, Paean, again bids go as bloody offerings to the monster the young men who had won the slaughter. O fortunate of soul, and worthy through the ages to deserve a long-remembered day! You do not, degenerate, hide your dutiful arms, nor tremble to meet a certain death. Bearing his face close, on the threshold of the Cirrhaean temple he stood, and roused the sacred wrath with these words: 'Not sent, Thymbraean, nor as a suppliant do I come to your household; my own piety and conscious valor have driven me these ways. I am he who by slaughter subdued, Phoebus, your mortal outrage, whom under black clouds and a squalid day, whom by the dark corruption of the sinister sky you seek, unjust one. But if savage monsters are so dear to the great gods, and the death of men is a loss cheaper to the world, and so great is the harshness in the cruel heaven, what have the Argives deserved? Me, me, best of the gods, me alone it were better to have set my head against the fates. Or is that more pleasing to your heart, that you see the dwellings of the homes desolate, and every field, its tillers given to the fire, shines? But why with talk do I delay your weapons and your hand? The mothers await, and the last vows are made for me. It is enough: I have deserved that you should not wish to spare. Therefore move your quivers, bend your sounding bows, and send down my notable soul to death; but that pale sphere which hangs above over Inachian Argos, while I die, drive it away.' An even lot looks upon the deserving: a reverence for the slaughter held back the burning son of Latona, and, humbled, he grants the man the sad honor of his life; the evil clouds flee from our sky, but you, entreated, go from the threshold of the astonished Phoebus. Thence these appointed rites are renewed every year with solemn feasts, and a new honor appeases the Phoebean temples. By chance you visit these altars — you, what offspring? Though Calydonian Oeneus and the rights of the house of Parthaon are yours, if rightly the cry went some while since to my ears: declare it, who you are who come to Argos, since these are the hours for various talk.'

Straightway the Ismenian hero cast his mournful gaze to the ground, and silently toward the wounded Tydeus turned his eyes aslant; then he broke his long silence: 'Not over these honors of the gods are you to ask of me whence my race, what land is mine, what order of ancient blood flows down: it shames me to confess it amid the sacred rites. But if your cares bid you to know my wretched self, Cadmus is the origin of my fathers, the Martial land is Thebe, Jocasta is my mother.' Then Adrastus, moved by the laws of hospitality — for he recognized him: 'Why hide what is known? We know,' he said, 'nor does fame roll so turned-away a course from Mycenae. The kingdom, and the furies, and the eyes that knew shame are known, and whoever shudders at the Northern suns, and whoever drinks the Ganges, or enters the dark Ocean at its setting, and any whom the Syrtes abandon on an uncertain shore. Cease to complain, and to number the misfortunes of those before you to yourself: in our blood too piety went much astray, nor does the fault bar the descendants. Only do you, unlike them, deserve in prosperous things to make excuse for your kin. And now, with the pole turned back, the icy carrier of the Hyperborean Bear grows faint. Pour wine on the hearths, and let us sing again and again in our vows of the son of Latona, the savior of our forefathers. Phoebus our father, whether the Patarean thickets of Lycia keep you on their snowy ridges, or it is your love to dip your golden locks in the chaste dew of Castalia, or whether you, the Thymbraean, hold Troy, where fame says you willingly bore the Phrygian millstones on your thankless shoulders, or whether the Latonian Cynthus delights you, striking the Aegean with its shadow, and you do not seek out Delos, constant on the sea: yours are the weapons, and the bow to be bent from afar against fierce foes, and to you the heavenly parents granted as a gift that your cheeks should flower forever; you, skilled to foreknow the unjust hands of the Fates and the fate beyond, and what will please highest Jove, what year is death-bringing, to what peoples wars, what scepters comets change; you bring the Phrygian beneath the lyre, you for your mother's honor stretch the earth-born Tityos out on the Stygian sands; green Python and the Theban mother shuddered at you exulting in your quiver; the avenging, grim Megaera for you presses fasting Phlegyas, lying beneath the hollow rocks, in an everlasting confinement, and goads him on with unholy feasts, but loathing mixed in conquers his hunger. Be present, O mindful of the welcome, and favor with your right hand the Junonian fields, whether it please you to be called rosy Titan in the manner of the Achaemenian race, or whether Osiris, the grain-bringer, is better, or Mithras, beneath the rocks of the Persian cave, who, indignant, twists the resisting horns.'

Meanwhile the winged son of Maia, bearing the commands of great Jove, returns from the icy shades; on every side the sluggish clouds forbid his going, and the turbid air entangles him. Nor did the west winds quicken his pace, but the foul breath of the silent pole. On one side Styx, flowing round its nine fields, on the other the opposing fires of torrents bar the ways. Behind, old Laius follows with trembling shade, still slow with his wound; for the impious sword went past his throat more deeply than the hilt, when by a kindred stroke it pierced his life through, and he bore the first wraths of the Furies; yet he goes on, and steadies his steps with the healing wand. Then the barren groves, the fields possessed by the dead, and the iron-gray wood stand astonished, and the Earth herself marvels that the way has opened backward; nor did the livid corruption of envy, though they were dead and now bereft of light, fail there. One among the rest, whose will was ever sinister, even toward those above — hence too his grievous end of life — who loved to insult misfortune and to sicken at glad things, 'Go,' he said, 'O fortunate, to whatever uses you are summoned, whether by Jove's command, or whether a greater Fury drove you to walk against the day, or whether the maddened Thessalian priestess bids you depart from your secret tomb, ah, to look upon the sweet skies and the abandoned sun, the green lands and the rivers clear at their springs, yet sadder still, again to enter into these shadows.' When Cerberus, reclining on the blind threshold, felt them, he raised all the gaping mouths of his heads, fierce even at the people entering; already his black neck swelled in menace, already he had scattered and stirred the bones on the ground, had not the god, soothing the bristling beast with a Lethaean branch, tamed his iron eyes with threefold sleep.

There is a place — the Inachian peoples have called it Taenarus — where the dreaded head of foaming Malea goes up into the airs and admits no gaze to its summit; the lofty peak stands serene, and looks down on the winds and the rains, and is only beset by the weary stars. There the exhausted winds have laid their couches, and there is a path for the lightnings; the hollow clouds have taken up the mountain's middle flank, and neither the clapping of the swift wing reaches the highest hills, nor do the hoarse thunders beat upon them. But when day is sloping, it casts long shadows over the seas, and a vast shade swims in the midst of the deep, Taenarus curves in its inner bay the breaking shores, not bold to climb the open waves. There, in the Aegean gulf, Neptune leads his weary horses down into harbor; the foremost hoof drinks up the sands, the hindmost fish-tails dissolve into the sea. In this place, as fame tells, a byway path drives the pale shades, and enriches the empty halls of dark Jove with the dead. If the Arcadian settlers tell the truth, there is the hissing and the groaning of punishments, and the field seethes with black tumult; often the voices and hands of the Eumenides have sounded into the broad day, and the doorkeeper of triple-formed Death, heard, has driven the farmers from the fields.

Here too then the winged god, covered with a dusky shade, leaps up to those above, and from his face shakes off the infernal clouds, and clears his features with the living breaths. Then through Arcturus and the silences of the mid-moon he travels over fields and peoples. Sleep, meeting him, was driving the horses of Night, and rises up trembling in honor of the deity, and gives way from the straight path of heaven; his shade flies lower than the god, who notes the stars forestalled and his own beginning; and now he looks down on lofty Cirrha and on Phocis, polluted with his own tomb. He had come to Thebes; near the threshold of his son Laius groaned, hesitating to enter the familiar household, but when he saw the yoke of his own car propped on the lofty columns, and the chariot still stained with blood, disturbed, he almost turns back: neither the highest commands of the Thunderer nor the breaths of the Arcadian wand hold him.

And then it chanced to be the day marked by the well-known thunderbolt of the Thunderer, when, tender Euhius, your birth, torn untimely, passed you to your father. To the Tyrian settlers this was a cause to draw out the sleepless night in eager play; poured out here and there through the houses, through the fields, amid garlands and bowls drained of wine, panting they breathed out the god under the dawn; then there was much boxwood pipe, and bronze cymbals overcoming with their din the beating of bulls. Cithaeron himself too, rejoicing through the wooded byways, had driven the sane mothers on with a kinder Bacchus; such banquets, in a maddened gathering, the Bistones set along Rhodope, or in the valleys of mid-Ossa. For them it is luxury to have a half-living beast and feasts shaken from the lions' mouth, and to have tamed their frenzy with new milk: but if ever the cruel scent of Ogygian Iacchus breathed upon them, then it is a fine thing to hurl stones with the hand, then the cups, and, with the undeserved blood of their fellows spilled, to renew the day and set the festal tables again.

That was the night when the winged Cyllenian, gliding on the silent air, sank to the bed of the Echionian king, where, huge, he had spread his limbs on the high couch piled with Assyrian tapestries. O mortal hearts, ignorant of their own fate! He takes the feast, he has his slumber. Then the elder does what he was bidden, and, lest the image of the night might seem false, he puts on the shadowy features of the aged prophet Tiresias, his voice and well-known fleece; the hair remained, and the white beard combed down upon the chin, and his own pallor; but a false fillet ran through the locks, and woven with gray-green olive came forth the honor of the bands: then he seemed to touch the breast with a branch and to utter these words of the fates: 'This is no time for sleep, slothful one, who in the deep night, heedless of your brother, lie idle; great deeds long since call you, and the grave preparations of affairs, you sluggard. You, just as if, when the south winds were already raising the great Ionian sea, the helmsman should lie beneath a black cloud, forgetful of his rigging and of the rudder that turns the waters, you delay. And now that other — Fame knows it — exults in a new marriage and prepares the strength by which to seize the kingdom, to deny it to you, and destines for himself old age in your hall. His father-in-law Adrastus, fated by augury, gives him courage, and Argos given as dowry; nor any less, into a bond for life, did Tydeus, stained with a brother's blood, find favor. Hence comes his pride, and as an exile he promises long things to your brother. The very father of the gods, pitying you, sends me from on high: hold Thebes, and your brother, blind with greed of the kingdom and ready to dare the same, drive him out; nor any longer, as he gapes for his brother's death, suffer him to trust to his undertaken frauds, or to bring imperious Mycenae against Cadmus.' He spoke, and drawing near — for now the horses of light were scattering the pale stars — he tore the branches and fleece from his brow, confessing the grandsire, and lay down upon his dread grandson's bed, then bares the throat gaping with slaughter, and drenches the sleep with the welling wound. His rest is broken; he raises his limbs and is snatched from the bed, full of monstrous sights, and shaking off the unreal gore, at once shudders at his grandsire and seeks his brother, as a tiger, when she has heard the murmur of hunters, bristles into her stripes and shakes off her sluggish slumbers; she longs for war, and loosens her jaws and tempers her claws, then rushes upon the squadrons and bears in her mouth a still-breathing man as food for her bloody young: so, roused by wrath, the leader spends his battles upon his absent brother.

And now, risen from her Mygdonian couches, Aurora had scattered the icy darkness high in the sky, shaking out her dewy locks and red with the much-following sun; for her, rosy through the clouds, the Morning Star turns his late flames and quits the alien aether on his slow horse, until the fiery father should fill the orb and forbid the rays even to his own sister: when the elder son of Talaus, and, after no long delay, the Dircaean and the Acheloian hero alike snatched their steps from their beds; those two, weary after the blows and the storm they had received, Sleep had drenched with all his horn; but for the Inachian king, beneath his breast a thin rest was drawn out, while in his mind he turns over the gods and the begun hospitality, and ponders what the fates may be, taken up with the kin he has found, after in the midst of the hall's seats they met and joined right hands in turn, and chose a place where it was fit to broach and unfold their secret cares, and sat down; first Adrastus addresses the doubtful ones thus: 'Excellent of young men, whom not without divine will the night with auspicious hand has brought into my realms, for whom my own Apollo, through the rains mingled with lightnings and the unseasonable Thunderer, made footsteps all the way to these dwellings, I do not think it obscure to you and to the Pelasgian people with what great zeal the crowd of suitors seek our marriage-ties; for to me two daughters — happy in grandchildren — grow up under an equal star. How great their honor and how great their modesty, believe not their father; even over yesterday's tables you could perceive it. These the proud men have desired, by their throne and by arms widely ruling — it were long to count up the Pheraean and Oebalian chiefs — and through Achaean towns the mothers, the hope of their race; nor did your Oeneus despise more treaties, a father-in-law to be feared with the Pisaean reins. But it is not lawful for me to join as sons-in-law men born of Sparta nor sent from Elis: for you this blood and the care of my hall are promised by a long order of fate. The gods are good, that you come of such stock and such spirit that the oracles are pleasing: this is the honor born in the time of the harsh night, this is that reward that came after the blows.' They had heard, and a little while held their eyes fixed on each other's faces, and seemed between themselves to yield in the order of speaking; but Tydeus, bolder in all his acts, begins: 'O how a ripe mind drives you, sparing of your own proclamation of fame, and how you tame with virtue the fortune that carries you! To whose commands would Adrastus yield? Who does not know that you, summoned from the throne of ancestral Sicyon, set unbridled Argos in order with your laws? And would that, just Jupiter, you might be willing to entrust to these hands the peoples that the Doric Isthmus binds within and that it sets apart below with its alternating shore! The broken light would not flee from dread Mycenae, nor would the Elean valleys groan with cruel contests, nor Furies upon Furies under different kings, and what you, Theban, have more cause to lament: but we indeed are willing and laid bare in spirit.' So he broke in, and the other adds: 'Would anyone refuse such fathers-in-law to draw near? Though for us, exiles driven from our country, Venus is not yet glad, yet all sadness has settled from the heart, and the griefs fixed in our mind have given way. Nor any the less gladly do we draw this solace, than if a ship, wrenched apart by the headlong south wind, should sight its friendly land; it gladdens us, having entered upon the happy omens of the kingdom, that whatever remains of fate and of life's labors should pass over by your fortune.' And delaying no more they rise; the Inachian father heaps up more lavishly with his words every promise, and pledges that he will be their aid and lead them back as restored to their fathers' realms.

Therefore Argos is eager: the rumor spread through the city that sons-in-law had come to the leader, and that at the first wedding-rites the noble Argia, and Deipyle, second to her in no praise of beauty, were now to be wedded in their swelling maidenhood; they prepare joy in their minds; Fame goes through the allied cities, and is stirred through the neighboring fields, far away as the Lycaean and Parthenian glades and over the Ephyraean lands; nor any less does the same turbulent goddess leap upon Ogygian Thebes, drenches these walls with her whole wings, and, in harmony with the night sent before, terrifies the Labdacian leader: the hospitality, the marriages, the bond of the kingdom, the mingled race — what such license has the monster, what madness? — and now she sings of war.

The awaited day had spread itself over Argos: the royal halls are filled with a glad gathering; one may behold the faces of the ancestors close at hand, and the bronze that vies with living features. That hands dared to bring such things to pass! The father Inachus himself, two-horned, sits leaning forward on his sloping urn on the left; him the aged Iasus covers, and placid Phoroneus, and the warrior Abas, and Acrisius, indignant at the Thunderer, and Coroebus bearing his head on a naked sword, and the grim image of Danaus now plotting his crime; then a thousand chiefs. Then through the proud doors the released wave of the crowd roars; every band of nobles, and they whose rank is nearer to the high king, stand in the first row in order. The inner hall grows warm with the rites and resounds with feminine tumult; the Argive women have girt the mother with a chaste crowd; some, poured around the maidens on every side, arrange the new bonds and soothe their fear. They went, conspicuous in face and in reverend bearing, crimson modesty poured over their white faces, and their cheeks downcast; silently there steals upon them that last love of maidenhood, and the modesty of the first fault confounds their faces; then their cheeks are wetted with honorable showers, and the tears gladdened their tender parents. Not otherwise than if, slipped down together from the heavenly gate, Pallas and the harsher sister of Phoebus, each with weapons, each grim of cheek and with a knot on her golden crown, the one should lead her companions on Cynthus, the other on Aracynthus; then, if it were lawful for the eyes, never by long gazing could you make out to which more honor, which more pleasing, or who has more of Jove. And should they wish to take on each other's exchanged dress, both the quivers would suit Pallas, and the crests the Delian.

The Inachidae contend in joy and weary the gods with vows, each according to his house and the means for sacrifice. These make offering with entrails and life, these with the bare turf; nor any the less, if the heart be accepted, are they heard to deserve the gods with incense, and they screen their thresholds with broken boughs. Lo, by a sudden fear — so hard Lachesis bade — their minds are struck, and joy is shaken from the father, and the day is troubled. They were approaching the unwedded Pallas on her threshold, to whom Argive Larissa, with its Monychian ridges, has not preferred any city: here, after the manner of their parents, the children of Iasus, when chaste youth ripened for the bridal-chamber, were used to dedicate their maiden locks and to make excuse for their first beds; as they were climbing the lofty citadel, the bronze disk, the spoil of Arcadian Euhippus, slips from the height of the topmost temple and falls upon the steps, and overwhelms the torches sent before, the festal fire for the brides, and from the remote shrines at the same time a huge trumpet, heard, terrified those who dared not yet steady their step. All, in their first dread, turned toward the king, then deny they heard it; yet upon all the dire omens of events work, and they increase their fear with various talk. No wonder: for then, your husband giving them, you wear, Argia, the ill-omened ornaments and the dread necklace of Harmonia. Long is the chain, but I will trace the known course of the evils, whence so cruel a power in the new gifts. The Lemnian wrought this, as the old faith holds, long grieving over the thefts of Mars; after, when no punishment stands in the way of his caught love, nor avenging chains chastised it, he had built, as Harmonia's dowry-glory, this for the bridal day. At this, though they labor at greater things, the skilled Cyclopes toil, and the Telchines, famed for their works, with friendly hand contended to help; but most of all his own sweat was spent. There he rings emeralds blooming with secret fire, and adamant, stamped with ill-omened figures, and Gorgon-orbs and the ashes of the last thunderbolt left on the Sicilian anvil, and the gleaming manes of green serpents from the forehead; here the mournful seed of the Hesperides, and the dire gold of the Phrixean fleece; then he weaves in various plagues, and a leader snatched from the black hair of Tisiphone, and what worst force approves of the cestus; this all around he cunningly anoints with lunar foam and steeps in a merry poison. Not Pasithea, first of the winsome sisters, not Beauty, nor the Idalian boy, but Grief and Wraths and Pain and Discord pressed it with her whole hand. The first proof of the work: Harmonia, having accompanied fallen Cadmus, her complaints turned to dread hissings, furrowed the Illyrian plains with her long breast. Soon wicked Semele scarcely put the harmful gifts upon her neck, and deceitful Juno entered her threshold. And you too, unhappy one, they say, Jocasta, possessed the lovely sin; with this glory she adorned her face, for what beds, alas, alas, she was to please! After it, a longer order. Then Argia shines with the gifts, and the worthless adornment of her sister, decked with sacred gold, comes over. The wife of the prophet doomed to perish had seen this, and before all the altars and the feasts she was secretly brewing a savage envy, whether at some time it might be granted her to possess the cruel adornments. Alas, in nothing helped by her near auguries. What groans she desires, what great calamities the impious one craves! Worthy indeed; but what did the deceived arms of her wretched husband, what did her innocent sons deserve of her frenzies?

After twelve days had closed the royal feasts and the joys of the people, the Ismenian hero began to look back toward Thebes and now to seek his own kingdom, for that day steals upon his mind, on which, by his brother's kindly lot, he had stood a private man in the Echionian hall, beholding the gods departed and his companions in trembling tumult scattered, all his flank bared, and the flight of fortune; for one sister alone dared to bring forth the mournful ways of the sad exile; even her he had left at the first threshold, and shut in his tears with mighty wrath. Then those he left glad as he went out, what was the chief adornment of the unjust leader, and which men, as he fled, he himself had marked to have groaned for him, through the night and under every day he reckons up: grief and mad wrath have eaten his spirit, and — than which no heavier care has been given to mortals — hope, when it comes after long delay; turning beneath his breast such a cloud of counsel, he prepares to go to Dirce and the denied homes of Cadmus, like a leader-bull, deprived of his loved valley, whom the herdsman, driven from his accustomed grass, has bidden bellow far from the heifer torn away, when, fleeing, his strength pleases him, and his neck returns great with recovered blood, and the oaks are broken upon his chest, he longs for war and demands back his pastures and the captured herd, now better with his foot, now with his horn — the victor himself dreads his returning, and the astonished masters scarcely knew him —: not otherwise did the Teumesian youth sharpen his silent wraths in his mind, but his faithful wife had felt his ways and his secrets; and as she lay, embracing her husband on the bed in the first paleness of dawn, 'What stirrings, cunning one, or what flight do you contrive?' she said: 'nothing escapes lovers. I feel it; sleepless sighs sharpen your complaints, never in peace is your sleep; how often do I catch this face swimming with weeping and your breast baying with great cares when I bring my hand near? Nothing, by the broken bond or by our marriage, moves me beyond, nor by a widowed youth, even though our love is raw, and the beds after the bridal torches have not yet grown warm throughout: it is your safety, I will hasten to confess it, that wrings me, beloved. Will you, unaccompanied, unarmed, seek the kingdom, and will you be able to depart your own Thebes, if he refuses? And fame, ever skilled to catch out leaders, tells that he is swollen and proud of what he snatched, and hard toward you: he has not yet spent the year. Me too now the seers, now the entrails threatening the gods, or the falling of birds, or the turbid image of night terrify, and — ah, I remember — never has Juno come to me false through the shadows. Where do you bend your way? Unless a conscious passion leads you, and a better father-in-law is at Thebes.' Here at last the Echionian youth smiled a little, and, consoling his wife's tender grief with an embrace, set timely kisses on her mournful cheeks and stayed her tears: 'Free your mind of fears; it will be granted, believe me, by the counsels of the deserving, a tranquil day; care too strong for your years does not yet become you. May the Saturnian father one day know these fates, and whatever eyes Justice cares to send down from the pole and to defend the right upon the earth: perhaps that light will come for you, on which you will see the walls of your husband, and go a queen through the twin cities.' So he speaks, and swiftly brings himself from the dear threshold.

Now Tydeus, already a partner in his undertakings, already with faithful heart matching his cares — so great a love, after their quarrels, bound their minds — he, sad, addresses his father-in-law Adrastus. There is delay in the counsel, when, as they move many things, one resolution at last sat better than all: to test the brother's faith and, by entreating, to explore safe approaches to the kingdom. Boldly does Tydeus take up this office of his own accord; nor any the less did Deipyle, with much weeping, try to delay you, most valiant of the Aetolian race; but the commands of her father, and the safety of his return in an envoy, and the just prayers of her sister prevailed.

And now, having measured the journey hard through woods and shore, where the Lernaean marsh and the hydra, burned deep in the shallows by the guilty, grows warm, and where Nemea, scarce with a rare song, sounds at length, the shepherds not yet daring, where the flank of Ephyre that slopes toward the eastern east winds, and the Sisyphean harbors lie, and the curving wave, angry at the land, is shut off by Palaemonian Lechaeum: sailing past from here, he leaves Nisus and you, gentle Eleusis, on his left, and now he enters the Teumesian fields and the Agenorean citadels; there he beholds harsh Eteocles lofty on his throne and hedged round with bristling arms. Fierce, he was giving laws to the people beyond the law and the seasons of his reign, now in his brother's part: he sits ready for every crime, and complains that faith is so late demanded back.

He stood in the midst — the olive branch shows the envoy — and, asked the causes of his journey and his name, declared them; and as he was ever rude in speech and prone to passion, yet mingling harsh things with just, he began: 'If plain faith and care for the treaty's word remained with you, it had been more just, the year completed, for envoys to go from here to your brother, and that you, in fixed order, should put off your fortune and gladly come down from the throne, so that he, long a wanderer and having suffered things unworthy through unknown cities, might at last succeed to the agreed hall. But because the love of the kingdom is sweet and power flattering, you are required: the swift circle has already turned the star-bearing orb, and the lost shadows have returned to the mountains, since your destitute brother through unknown towns drives out his sad fortunes as an exile; and it is now time for you to bear the days under the open sky, and to lead through your limbs the chill of the earth, and humbled to court a stranger's household. Set a limit to your joys; rich enough in purple and gold, conspicuous, you have mocked the meager year of your poor brother; I warn you, unlearn for yourself the joys of kingdoms, and patient of exile earn the right to return.' He had spoken; but in him long since beneath his silent breast the fiery heart roars, as a fierce serpent, struck by a thrown stone, rears up close at hand, in whose empty hidden depths beneath a long thirst, stirred through all its frame, summons the venom into its jaws and scaly neck: 'If my brother's quarrels had been known to me before by doubtful signs, and the clear secrets of his hatred had not lain open, even faith alone would suffice, by which, grim and bearing him too in his mind, as a new besieger now loosens the walled ramparts and the war-trumpets make his squadrons enemies, you are raging. If at close quarters you had carried your speech among the Bistones, or the Geloni pale with the retreating sun, you would have begun more sparing of eloquence and more reverent of the middle fair. Nor would I charge you with the crime of a furious mind: you bear another's commands. Now, since all is full of threats, and you demand the scepter neither in faith nor with peace as mediator, and your hand is closer to the hilt, carry back these words, spoken to the Argive king — not yet equal to yours — in my turn: the lot that is just to me, the scepter that an honor not unowed to my years has dedicated, I hold and will long hold. With you let the Inachian palace, given as the dowry of your wife, and the wealth of Danae — for why should I envy greater deeds? — be heaped up; under happy auspices may you rule Argos and Lerna; for us the rough pastures of Dirce and the shores cramped by Euboean waves, not having scorned to call wretched Oedipus our father: yours the ample nobility — Pelops and Tantalus your founders! — and a nearer Jove may flow to you from joined blood. Or will the queen, accustomed to her father's luxury, bear this hearth? For whom should our sisters by right draw the anxious wool-tasks, or the mother, foul with long mourning, and that holy old man, perhaps heard from the lowest shadows, offend her? Already the hearts of the crowd are used to the yoke; it shames me, alas, both of commons and of fathers, lest so often they should bear uncertain rule and, groaning, change it, and be loath to obey a doubtful tyrant. A brief reign does not spare its peoples; consider how great the dread, and how the citizens are astonished at our crisis! Shall I, then, leave these men, for whom under you as leader the penalty is sure? Angry, brother, you come; suppose you are willing: not even the fathers, if only my love is known and the grace of my desert, will suffer me to give back the kingdom.' He suffered no more, and threw his words across into the midst of the speech: 'You will give it back,' he repeats, 'you will give it back: not if an iron rampart should ring you round, or if Amphion, heard with another song, should drive triple walls for you, shall any weapons or fires prevent you from paying for your daring, and beneath our arms, dying, from beating the ground with your captive diadem, you justly; but I pity these men, whom, cheap of blood, torn from their wives and children to unspeakable battles, you cast forth, good king, to ruin. O what great funerals will Cithaeron, and you, bloody Ismenos, roll in your floods! This is your piety, this your great faith! Nor do I indeed hold the crimes of your race a marvel: so was the first author of the blood, and the incestuous beds of the fathers; but the origin is deceptive: you alone were of Oedipus — these rewards of your character and crime you will bear, while he looks on! We ask for the year; but I delay.' These things, bold, still on the threshold, crying out backward, headlong then through the thronged ranks he flies forth. So that avenger of Oenean Diana, bristling with hairs and with the lightning of his curved jaw, when the Pelopian phalanx pressed him, rolling the rocks before him and the Acheloian thickets broken from the dug-through banks, now leaving Telamon on the ground, now Ixion laid low, comes upon you, Meleager: there at last he stuck in the broad spear-point and slackened his rage on the resisting shoulder. Such did the Calydonian hero leave the still-trembling council, gnashing his teeth, as though the kingdom were denied to himself, and hastens his way, and casts away the entreating branch of olive; from the topmost threshold of the dwellings the astonished mothers look on, and pray unspeakable things against the cruel son of Oeneus, and, in their silent breast, against the king at once.

Nor is the leader, ready in the genius of crime and of unspeakable fraud, in want. The faithful of his youths, bodies most choice for war, now with reward, now blazing with their own urgings, he stirs up with words, and cruelly arranges a battle by night, and to invade the name, holy to peoples through the ages, of an envoy with treachery and silent steel — what is not cheap to kingdoms? — he longs; what arts he would seek, Fortune, if you gave him his brother! O blind counsels of the guilty! O ever-fearful crime! The people goes out, sworn by the steel, against a single head; as if to assault a camp it makes ready, or to bring down the lofty flank of a city by the frequent blows of the ram: so, a column made, fifty are poured out in order from the high gates. A blessing on your spirit, worthy to be trusted with such great arms!

A nearer way leads through the thickets, where by a hidden path they hasten ahead and choose the shortcuts of the dense wood. A seat is chosen for the treachery: far from the city, twin hills press close with their malign gorges, which the shade of the lofty mountain and the leafy ridges shut in with their curving woods — nature has built ambush in the place and a blind aid for hiding — and a rough path cuts the rocks artfully between, beneath which the plains and the lands sloping in broad spaces lie; opposite is an unwelcome ledge, the home of the winged thing of Oedipus; here the wild beast once, with her pale cheeks upraised and her eyes suffused with gore, her feathers clotted with unspeakable blood, embracing the remains of men and pressing to her bare breast the half-eaten bones, stood, and with a terrible gaze scanned the fields, if any guest dared to contend with her unsolved sayings, or any traveler to go hand to hand and join an exchange with her dire tongue; nor was there delay, but at once, sharpening her outthrust claws and her livid hands and her teeth drawn for wounds, with a terrible clapping she rose around the stranger's face; and her wiles lay hidden, until from the bloody rock — alas! — caught by a man like these, her wings failing, sad she dashed her unsatisfied belly upon the crags. The wood points out the abomination: the bullocks dread the neighboring grass, the greedy flock keeps from the accursed herbs; the shade pleases not the choirs of Dryads, nor is it fit for the rites of the Fauns, and even the dire birds have fled the portentous grove. Driven here with silent steps the cohort doomed to perish comes down, and, against the proud foe, leaning on their javelins and holding their arms laid on the ground, they wait, and crown the wood with a dense outpost.

Night had begun to weave Phoebus with her damp robe and had poured the dark-blue shade over the lands; he was drawing near the woods, and from the high bank sees the shields of men and the helmets with their crests redden. Where the branches loosen the wood, and in the shade facing him a flame-colored quiver of the moon wanders over the brazen arms, he was amazed at the sight; yet he went on; only he brings up his bristling spear and the sword enclosed up to the hilt, and first, 'Whence, men, or why hidden in arms?' he asks with no humble dread; nor is a voice returned against him, and the suspicious silences deny a trustworthy peace. But lo, hurled from the vast arm of Chthonius, on whom the cohort relied as leader, a spear flies through the dusky air; but the god and fortune withdrew from him as he dared. Yet through the covering of Olenian boar's-hide and the back black with bristles, above his left shoulder, near to dying, it escaped, and struck his throat in vain with the widowed wood. Then his hair stood up and his blood was frozen in his heart. Bearing his spirit fierce this way and that, and his face pale with wrath — nor does he think so great a war prepared for him —: 'Bring your steps against me and burst out into the open field! What fear of daring, what such cowardice? Alone, alone I call to arms.' Nor in this is there delay: when he sees them, more than he had reckoned, run out from countless lairs, these advancing from the ridges, those from the lowest valleys growing up, and not a few in the plain, and the whole way gleaming with arms, as the first voice brings forth into the open the beasts shut in by the net, when the way of healing is troubled and confused by reason alone, he seeks the heights of the dread Sphinx, and breaking the lines on the sheer cliffs, surmounts the dire ridges, and, master of a crag, whence far behind is dread and a sloping way of harming, a huge rock, which the groaning bullocks could scarcely turn from the ground with full neck and bring to the walls, he tears from the rocks; then, straining with all his blood, he holds it up, seeking to balance the monstrous ruin, as great-souled Pholus raised the empty mixing-bowl against the Lapiths who faced him. The throng, doomed to death, stands amazed at him standing over them, and is overwhelmed by the whirlwind of the loosed mountain; at once the faces of the men, at once their arms and hands, and the broken breasts, settled mingled with the iron. Four here, scattered beneath one mass, groaned together; the column, straightway shaken with terror, is thrown by flight from its undertaking, for the funerals that lay there were not to be despised: lightning-like Dorylas, whom a blazing valor matched with kings, and Theron of the seed of Mars, trusting in his earth-born grandsires, and Halys second to none in turning the reins — but now he lies a footman in the fields — and Phaedimus, dragging Pentheus, not yet your equal, Bacchus, in race. When the squadrons, terrified by these sudden fates, saw the disordered band loosen its throng, the two javelins alone which he had fixed, holding them in his hand, leaning against the mountain, he hurls and adds to the fleeing. Soon he gladly is carried headlong down with a leap onto the plain, lest the weapons should fall on his bare breast, and seizes the disk which he had seen rolled far off when Theron was crushed, and, hedged about back and crown with the well-known coverings, and defending his breast with the enemy's shield, he took his stand. Then again the children of Ogyges gather densely into one and steady their step; more swiftly Tydeus draws his Bistonian sword, the Martial gift of great Oeneus, and, divided alike into all parts, goes against these and those, and with his steel strikes down the flashing weapons; they hinder themselves by their number, and their own arms in turn press on one another, nor is there any force in their efforts, but their very hands stray against their fellows, and the bodies, slipping, are wrapped in their own throng; he, narrow amid them, abides the rushing weapons, and stands unconquerable in the way, not otherwise — if it is lawful to believe in Getic Phlegra — than immense Briareus stood against the armed aether, on this side the quivers of Phoebus, on that the serpent of grim Pallas, thence the Pelethronian pine of Mars with its fixed point, and on this side scorning the bolts changed by weary Pyracmon, when, beset in vain by all Olympus, he complains that so many hands are idle: no less keenly does Tydeus burn, thrusting his shield this way and that, and, withdrawing, he himself circles round; at times he meets the trembling foes and presses, plucking out the darts which, many over his whole shield, stick quivering and arm the man, though often he suffers harsh wounds; but he can hope for no entrance into the secret parts of life, nor for death.
