Then indeed, astonished at the highest hinge of the fates, as if the final plague should come upon the city, and Bellona, about to level the towers to the ground with bloody torches, were entering, from all the roofs they vie to whirl huge stones and oaks and the strong thongs of the Balearic sling — for whence is hope in javelins and arrows wandering in the sky? — but eagerly they whirl their engines too and press with masses. He, never dragged down by the weapons hurled before or following upon his back, and hanging in the empty air as if treading the level ground with sure footsteps, strains on and climbs against the vast ruin that meets him: as a river, pressing against the timbers of an old bridge, assails them with ceaseless waters, now the stones crack and the beams are dislodged; so much the more violent he — for he feels it — shakes and drags with a greater surge the sick mass, until the swift channel cuts off all its bonds, and the victor breathes again in his open course; and when, lofty, he rose above the long-sought heights and, rising, looked down upon the trembling city and terrified Thebes with his huge shadow, he upbraids the astonished men: 'The humble citadels of Amphion, for shame! These walls, pliant and following an unwarlike song, these, the long-lying fable of Thebes? And what glory to lay low walls built by a soft lyre?' At once, insulting with foot and hand, he savagely pulls down the wedges and planking that bar his way: the bridges leap apart, and the stony stays of the pressing roof give way, and using again the broken-down mound, he hurls the shattered crags upon the temples and houses and breaks the city with its own walls.

And now around Jove the Argive and the Tyrian gods raged with divided zeal; the father, just to both, beholds their great wraths near at hand, ablaze, and sees himself stand in their way, he groans with his stepmother looking on, Liber, and looking back at his father with sidelong eye: 'Now where is your savage hand, and, alas, my flame's cradle, the bolt — ah, where is the bolt?' he says. Apollo groans for the homes that he himself gave; mournful, the Tirynthian weighs Lerna against Thebes and hesitates with bent bow; the winged son of Danaë laments his mother's Argos; Venus weeps for the people of Harmonia, and, fearing her husband, stands afar and looks back at Gradivus with silent wrath. Bold Tritonia upbraids the Aonian gods, furious silences torment Juno, who keeps still. Yet these things do not trouble the peace of Jove: lo, the quarrels have ceased, when Capaneus is heard amid the stars. 'Do you stand, you powers, for trembling Thebes?' he cried. 'Where are the sluggish nurslings of that unspeakable land, Bacchus and Alcides? It shames me to provoke the lesser ones. You rather come — for who is worthier to clash with us? Look, the ashes and the tomb of Semele are held — now come, now strive against me with all your flames, Jupiter! Or are you braver to trouble timid girls with thunder and to raze the towers of Cadmus, your father-in-law?'

The grief of the gods groaned at his words; Jove himself laughed at the raving man, and shaking the mass of his sacred hair: 'What hope is there for men after the battles of swelling Phlegra! Must you too be struck?' he says. On every side the crowd of gods presses the slow one, gnashing, and demands the avenging weapons, nor does his wife now dare, troubled by the fates, to withstand, the heavenly palace itself, the signal not yet given, of its own accord thunders, the very clouds gather without wind and the rains hurry up: you would think Iapetus had broken his Stygian chains, or that bound Inarime or Aetna were being lifted to the upper vaults; the dwellers of heaven are ashamed to fear these things; but when amid the whirl of the world they see the man stand and demand his mad battles, they marvel in silence and grow pale at the doubtful bolt. Above the heights of the Ogygian tower the pole had begun to bellow secretly, and the sky to be taken in darkness: yet he holds the citadels he does not see, and as often as the lightnings flashed from the grinding storms, 'This way,' he says, 'to Thebes, with these fires now it is fit to use, hence to renew the brands and kindle my weary oak.' As he spoke such things, the bolt, driven with all of Jove, seized him: his foremost crests fled into the clouds, and the black boss of his shield falls, and now all the limbs of the man shine. The lines give way, and on both sides the terror, where he may rush, what squadrons he may strike with his burning body, he feels the brand hiss within him, his helmet and his hair, and trying with his right hand to thrust off the burning breastplate, he handles the ash of the iron beneath his breast. Yet he stands, and turned toward the stars he breathes his last, and thrusts his smoking breast against the hated walls, that he might not fall: but his earthly limbs leave the man, and his spirit is put off; if a little more slowly his limbs had given way, he might have hoped for a second bolt.

After great-souled Capaneus had spent the frenzies of an unjust valour and breathed out the bolt he had taken in, and the path of the avenging flame had marked the walls, having attended his far fall to earth: the victor Jupiter sets in order with his right hand the shaken strokes of his blows, and brings back the sky and the day with his face. The gods give thanks, as though, wearied, he panted from the battles of Phlegra and had pressed smoking Aetna upon Enceladus. He lies clasping the fragments of the torn tower, grim still to see, and leaving deeds to be remembered by the nations and not unpraised even by the Thunderer himself. As great as the violator of Apollo's mother is stretched in Avernus; the very birds shudder, if ever from his deep breast they emerge, and they gaze at the immense limbs of him as he lies, while the wretched fibres grow into their fodder: so, cast there, he weighs upon the earth and burns the hostile fields and the plain that pants with celestial sulphur, Thebes breathes again, and from the temples the fallen ranks rise; now there is an end to vows and an end to their last laments, and the mothers dared to set down their children.

But wandering flight rolled the Achaeans straggling over the field. No longer are the enemy squadrons or mortal iron feared: before all eyes is the wrath of Jove, for all their arms blaze with fear and their helmets thunder, and they think Jupiter himself pursues them and sets fires against the fleeing. The Agenorean soldier presses on, and uses the tumult of the sky: as when through the Massylian fields a lion has broken the untamed kings of the herd with his great jaws and goes off content; then close at hand the harsh bears, then the greedy wolves come, and, their rage relaxed, they lick, degenerate, the wounds of another's prey. Here Eurymedon presses on, with rustic dread upon his arms, rustic weapons in his hand, and his father's way of stirring tumults: Pan was his sire; here Alatreus, a boy, surpasses in his attempts his tender years and matches his youthful father: happy both, but more fortunate is he whom it gladdens to have begotten; nor now is it easy to tell apart which arms ring louder, from which arm the spear flies farther.

The rampart is crowded with the dense swarm of the fleeing, what turns do you roll, Gradivus? Just now they were scaling the walls of Cadmus: now the Pelasgians defend their own dwellings! As the clouds come back, as with the south winds blowing about the field bends down by turns, as in the white whirlpool now the tide uncovers the thirsty sands, now clothes them. Far and wide the Tirynthian band breathes its last, the offspring that copied the spoils of the god; grim from the stars mourns Amphitryon's son, to see in blood the Nemean hides and the like clubs and the like quivers. On the iron-bound height of an Argive tower there stood Enyeus, peerless with the war-trumpet of Mars favouring him, the encourager; but then he was giving the wretched a useful signal and counselling flight and safe retreats into the camp: when a sudden wound came down from the slanting air, and his left hand was held to his ear, catching the sound that pressed it, just as it was; now his spirit flees into the empty breezes, now his cold lips are silent, the trumpet alone finished the song.

And now Tisiphone, mistress of crimes and practiced in the blood of a twofold race, seeks to mock the fraternal war in the line of battle: nor does she trust herself enough for so great a contest, unless she rouse her companion Megaera from her infernal seat and her kindred snakes to the battle, therefore she withdraws afar into an empty valley, and digs the ground with her Stygian sword, and absent murmurs into the earth a name and — an unmistakable sign to the Elysian realms — lifts a horned serpent from her hair with a long hiss: that leader of the dark-blue locks, at whose sound forthwith all the earth and the sea and the pole shuddered, and the father looked back again to the fires of Aetna, she receives the sound; by chance she stood then closest to her parent, while in all the assembly of Dis Capaneus is praised and she cherishes the shade marked out by the Stygian streams, forthwith, the mass of the earth broken open, beneath the stars she stood, the dead exult, and as much as the deep darkness thinned out, so much did the light recede. Her black sister receives her and, clasping her right hand, speaks:

'Thus far, sister, I have been able to bear the dread commands of our Stygian parent and the frenzies bidden me, alone above the earth and a victim meeting the world, while you restrain Elysium and the gentle shades. Nor is the reward of my delay ugly, nor my labours empty: all this, that the fields are wet, that the pools steam with blood, that the Lethaean bank rejoices in its countless swarm, is my strength, my glad insignia; but why do I speak of these? Let Mars have them, and let common Enyo boast them. You saw — surely it was plain among the Stygian shades — the leader foul with blood, his open jaws and his face wet with black gore: the wretch devours insatiably the head I gave him; just now indeed a dreadful crash came down to you from the stars: a sacred tempest pressed upon me, I, mingled in the frenzied arms of the man, was watching the wars of the gods and the great wraths of the bolt. But now — for I will speak it — with long toil my heart grows weary, sister, and my hands are slow; the nether yew dulls in the sky, and the too-many stars lull my unwonted snakes. You, in whom all the fury still is, and whose locks exult, fresh from the spring of Cocytus, grant me to join my strength, no accustomed lines nor wars of Mars do we prepare, but the brothers' — though kindly Faith and Piety resist, they shall be conquered — the brothers' swords must be drawn hand to hand, a great work! Let us ourselves be fitted with hatreds, ourselves with discordant arms. Why do you come so slow? Come, choose whose standards you will carry; both are easy and ours; but the doubtful crowd, and the addresses of the mother, and Antigone, coaxing with her prayers, I fear, lest a little they delay our counsels; even he himself, who was wont to weary us with his praying and to demand the avenging Furies of his eyes, is now a father: he is said now to weep alone, apart from all the company, for his own. And indeed I myself delay to burst into Thebes and the accustomed hearth; let the impious exile obey you, and drive on the Argive crime; let not mild Adrastus prevail, beware, nor the Lernaean folk delay him, go, and turn back, an enemy, to the alternating fights.'

Having so divided their tasks, the sisters went their separate ways: as Notus and Boreas from the twin poles of the world, this one fed on Rhipaean snow, this one on Libyan sands, stir wars: the rivers cry out, the seas, the clouds, the woods, and now the ruins lie open; the farmers bewail their losses, and yet they pity the sailors caught upon the sea. When the father, high on the summit of Olympus, saw those two defiling the day, and Hyperion's trembling orb suffused with stains, he begins thus with a grim face: 'I have seen the arms-bearing frenzies, as far as right allowed, dwellers of heaven, and the lawful battle-lines, though one man entered upon impious war and dared to fall by my right hand, now an unspeakable match and a combat unknown to the wretched lands draws near: take away your eyes! Let them dare those things with the gods absent, and be hidden from Jove; enough to have seen the banquets of Tantalus and the guilty altars of Lycaon and Mycenae leading the swift stars to the pole. Now even the day must be troubled: receive, earth, evil clouds, and let the poles withdraw: it is resolved to spare the world and my heavenly ones; at least let not the stars of the kindly maiden, nor the brothers of Leda, see such things.' So the almighty father, and he took away their sight from the guilty fields, and the earth lacked the sweet clear sky.

And now the maiden, child of Erebus, traces Polynices' course through the Argive cohorts, and finds it close beneath the gates, uncertain whether by death or by unjust flight he should go out, and omens had troubled his doubtful senses: he had seen, while in the dark night he wandered the rampart, sick of counsel and turning over his last cares, the torn image of his wife Argia with a mournful torch — there are portents of the gods, thus she was making ready to go, to carry such brands to her husband! — therefore as he asked what way, what grief, why the mournful tokens, she had only wept, and with her hand had turned away the silent fires, he knows his mind has seen a horror; for from where would she come from Mycenae, and the wife, unlooked-for, approach the rampart? But he feels the warnings of fate and the funerals near, and fears to feel them, when indeed the Dira of opened Acheron, plying her lash three times, touched his breastplate, he burns, helpless in spirit, and not so much to sit upon the throne as to commit crime and slaughter, and amid the blood of his pierced brother to breathe his last, does he desire, and suddenly he addresses Adrastus:

'Late indeed, the last surviving of the allies and of the Argive race, I undertake counsels, father, when affairs are already in straits; then was the time, when the blood of the Achaeans was whole, to go forth of my own will and take up my proper fight, not to expose the flower of the Danaan people and the venerable souls of kings, that I might put upon my head a lamentable honour for so many cities; since the rough season of valour has passed, now at least let it be right to pay what I have deserved; for you know, father-in-law, though you hide deep your wounds and respect the broken shame of your son-in-law: I am that man who drove you, ruling peace and pious laws — unhappy I, and would I had been given as a guest to other cities! — an exile from your country and kingdom — but at last exact the penalty: my brother to the final war — why do you shudder? it is decreed and fixed — I summon; cease to delay, nor will you be able, not if my black mother and my wretched sisters fall into the midst of arms, not if my father himself stand against me as I rush to war and thrust his quenched orbs upon my helmet, shall I fail. Or shall I drink whatever of Inachian blood remains, and even now make use of your deaths? I saw the chasms of the earth burst open for my sake, and did not enter; I saw Tydeus lifeless and made him guilty; undefended Tegea demands me back, her king, and my bereaved mother howls for me in the Parrhasian caves, I myself could neither climb the banks of Ismenos, while Hippomedon made the pools bloody, nor the Tyrian towers, while it thundered, and share the frenzies with you, Capaneus, what so great fear for the light have I? But I shall pay worthy recompense. Let them gather, wherever each is, the Pelasgian wives and mothers and aged fathers, whose joys I plucked so many and whose homes I bereaved: I run against my brother, what is there beyond? Let them watch, and with their vows demand Eteocles the victor. And now farewell, my wife, and farewell, sweet Mycenae! But you, dear father-in-law — for not all the blame of my woes is mine, and the gods are with me, and the guilty Fates — be gentle to my ashes, and when after this battle I am snatched by the birds, cover me from my brother and bring my urn back home — this only — and join your daughter in a better marriage.'

They were dissolving into tears, as when, spring returned, the Bistonian snows grow warm, and the huge Haemus is lowered, and Rhodope sinks into narrow streams, and the old man had begun to soothe the raging one with gentle address: the bloody Fury cut short his words with new terror, and the swift-footed horse and the fatal arms, forthwith, having taken on the face of Inachian Phereclus, she offered, and shut out the faithful voices with the helmet. And besides: 'Break off the delays, let us hasten! And they say he is approaching the gates.' So she overcame all things, and seizing him flung him upon the horse; he flies over the open plain, pale, and looks round at the goddess' shadow pressing him.

The Tyrian leader, deeming he had disarmed the Danaans, was bearing sacrifices, in vain, to Jove for the bolt, as was due, nor was the heavenly father or any of the gods at these altars, but evil Tisiphone, inserted among the trembling ministers, stands near, and forestalls the vows for the infernal Thunderer. 'Highest of the gods, for to you the origin of my Thebes — though unspeakable Argos and harsh Juno may envy it — is owed, ever since you, a ravisher, along the Sidonian shores troubled the dances, deigning to be pressed by our maiden's back and falsely to bellow through the calm waves! Nor is it a vain belief that you again won a Cadmean marriage and burst, too much, into the Tyrian household: at last, I say, gracious, you look back at your kinsmen and your beloved walls, and as their champion you thunder; as if the royal court of your own heaven were assailed, so for our high towers we saw you driving the clouds, and glad we recognize the kindly bolt and the fires our forefathers heard. Receive now the flocks and the great heaps of incense and the vowed male; but to render worthy thanks is no mortal work; let our Bacchus and Alcides vie to repay you, for them you keep these walls.' He had spoken: but a black fire leaped onto his face and cheeks, and snatching the diadem from his hair burned it. Then the fierce bull before the stroke stains the shrines with foam, and bursts from the midst of those who bar it, in tumult, carrying off the altars with its maddened horn. The servants scatter, and the soothsayer consoles the king, he himself, ill-emboldened, orders the rite to be renewed and performed, and with a feigned face presses down his great fears, as when the Tirynthian felt the fire wrapped about his bones and the Oetaean garments closing upon his limbs, yet bore on the vows begun and the incense poured, hard still and patient of his evil; soon, compelled, he groaned aloud, and victorious Nessus rages through his vitals.

A messenger, his breast in suspense from his breathless course, Aepytus, his post at the gate abandoned, makes for the king and pants out this, scarcely understood in his alarm: 'Break off your pious worship and the untimely rites of the gods, ruler: your brother presses on all the walls about, and assails the delays of the gates with rein and spears, demanding you by name, again and again, you alone for battle.' Behind, the mournful companions weep, and each groans at his words, and the army murmurs back with clashing arms, he cries: 'Now was the time, best father of the gods! What did Capaneus deserve?' Troubled, the king shuddered with deep hatreds, and yet rejoiced amid his wrath. So when the ruling bullock, after the leisure of the exiled bull, has caught with the top of his ear the hostile bellowing and recognized the threats, he stands seething with great wrath before the herd and breathes out his courage with burning foam, now grim cleaving the earth with his foot, now the air with his horns; the field shudders, and the trembling valleys await the battle.

Nor do the companions of the kingdom fail: 'Let him batter the walls in vain.' 'But shall he dare so far, his strength broken?' 'It is a wretched madness to press upon danger, and not to weigh fears and to hate what is safe.' 'Stay here, trusting in your throne, we will repel the enemy, bid us make war.' So the crowd nearest him; but blazing, lo, Creon was at hand, in grief, and about to speak all things with the freedom of war: Menoeceus burns his fierce heart; no rest for the father, he both seeks him and holds him; he beholds him breathing rivers of blood from his breast and forever falling from the savage tower. When he saw Eteocles doubtful and delaying the fight: 'You will go,' he says, 'nor will we any longer endure unavenged you, worst of men, both brother and leader, mighty in the funerals and the tears of your country, guilty of the Furies and of the war. Enough have we paid for your perjuries to the unjust gods. A city heavy with arms and wealth and lately crowded with citizens, as a plague cast down from heaven or a hostile land, you have drained, and yet, lofty, overshadow its emptiness? The people fail you for your service: these the ground bears, wanting fire; these the native river has already carried down to the sea; these search for limbs, those tend their anxious wounds, give back, come, to the wretched their brothers and sons and fathers, give back their men to the fields and the homes! Where is mighty Hypseus and neighbouring Dryas, where the arms of resounding Phocis and the Euboean leaders? Yet the equal lot of war bore them to the shades: but you — for shame! — a victim of the kingdom, a victim, son, you lie, like dumb blood from the herd, ah me! by the first-fruits of the altars and by a duly accursed rite poured out and bidden to die; and will that man delay further, nor now at least, summoned by hostile Mars, take his stand? Or does profane Tiresias bid another go to the battles, and again weave his oracles into my groans? For what but Haemon, the only one, remains to me, wretched? Bid him go forth, and you sit here a spectator from the high tower! Why do you growl savagely and look back at your servile cohort? These wish you to go, these to pay the penalty; your very mother and your very sisters hate you. Against you your blazing brother threatens iron and death and assails the impious bars of the gates, and do you not hear?' So the father, gnashing, and boils with wretched wrath. He at this: 'You do not deceive,' he says, 'nor do your son's glorious fates move you: to chant and to boast of those was fitting for a father, but hope hides beneath your tears, hope and hidden longing lurks in these words: you set forth funerals before me with insane prayer, and press me in vain, as one nearest to an empty hall, not so will Fortune have left the Sidonian city, that the sceptre should fall to you, most unworthy of so great a son. Nor is the present revenge hard for me; but arms, arms first, servants! Let the brothers meet in battle, Creon wishes to ease his groans: gain your fury; when I am victor, you shall pay for all.' So for a little he put off the quarrel, and the sword which his anger already offered, he checked. As a serpent, struck by a shepherd's uncertain wound, rears in a coil and gathers from its whole body the long venom into its mouth; if a little the foe, going wide, has turned his path, the threats fall and the swollen neck sinks in vain, and it drinks the wraths of its own poison itself.

But the mother, when, frantic, she first dreaded the rumour of the deadly lot — nor did she believe it slowly — went with her hair torn and her face, and her breast bare and bloody, mindful neither of sex nor of seemliness: as the Penthean mother climbed the heights of the maddened mountain, about to bring the promised head to savage Lyaeus. Not her companions, not the dutiful steps of her daughter have equal power to bear it: only her last grief gives the wretched woman strength, and her bloodless years grow fierce with mourning. And now the leader was fastening the ornament of his helmet, now the savage points, and was looking out for his horse, glad and undismayed at the war-trumpets and the clarions, when suddenly the great mother appeared, and he himself paled with fear, and the whole company of servants, and the armour-bearer drew back the offered spear. 'What madness? Whence again does the renewed Fury of the kingdom rise up? Will you yourselves too, after all, you yourselves stand hand to hand? Is it so little to have led the twin cohorts and commanded the crime? Where then will the victor return? Into this bosom? O happy darkness of my grim husband long ago! You pay the penalty, wicked eyes; is this the day to be watched? Whither, savage one, do you turn your threatening face? Why does your countenance change with alternating pallor and flush, and why do your set teeth grind out evil murmurs? Wretched me, you will conquer! But first you must needs make trial of these arms at home: I will stand on the very threshold of the gate, an unlucky omen and a monstrous image of crimes. This grey hair, these breasts, accursed one, you must trample, and through your mother's womb this steed must be driven, spare me: why do you thrust me off, set against your hilt and shield? I did not against you sanction deadly vows to the Stygian gods, nor with blind mouth ask the Erinyes. Hear your wretched mother: your mother, savage one, prays you, not your father; add delay to crime, and measure what you dare, but your brother batters the walls and stirs impious war against you. For no mother, no sister stands in his way as he goes; all things beg you, here we all lament, but there scarcely one, Adrastus, dissuades the fight, or perhaps commands it: do you leave your ancestral thresholds and gods and go from our embraces against your brother?'

But from the other side, by stealth, amid the opposing tumult, Antigone stole her steps — nor did chaste virginity hold her back — and flies, raging, to surmount the height of the Ogygian wall; an aged companion clings to her as she goes, Actor, who would not endure to the topmost citadel, and when from afar she hesitated a little at the arms she saw, and recognized — horror! — him assailing the roofs with javelins and proud voice, first she fills all with great lamentation, and from the walls, as if about to descend, speaks out: 'Hold your weapons in your hand and look a little back at this tower, brother, and turn your bristling crests upon my eyes, do you recognize your enemies? Is it thus we demand the yearly compact and the faith? These the complaints, this the good cause of a modest exile? By the Argive household gods, my brother, through you — for to the Tyrians there is now no honour — and by whatever in that home is sweet, lower your spirit: lo, both the throngs of the race beg you, and both the lines; she begs you, Antigone, devoted to the woes of her own and suspected by the king, and your sister at least, hard one; loosen your face and your grim cheeks; let it be granted perhaps for the last time to know the features I love and to see whether at these laments you weep; him already with suppliant groan the mother breaks, and is said to be letting fall the drawn sword: are you still brave for me? For me, who weep your exiles and wanderings night and day, and have so often soothed for you our father, even now swelling with wrath? With what charge do you free your brother? Surely he broke faith and the fixed treaties, he is the guilty one, savage to his own; yet, lo, summoned, he does not come.' At these words the fury had begun a little to grow faint, though the Erinys clamoured and resisted; now his hand is lowered, now slowly he turns the reins, now he is silent; the groans burst forth, and the helmet confesses his tears; his wraths grow dull, and alike to depart guilty and to have come shames him: when suddenly, the mother thrust back, the Fury flung Eteocles forth through the broken gates, crying: 'I come, and only this, that you called me first, I begrudge; do not chide the delay, the mother gripped my heavy arms; ah, my country, O most uncertain land of kings, now surely you shall belong to the victor!' nor more gently he at last said: 'You know, savage one, your faith, and come down to fair ground? O now for the first time, after a long while, my brother, meet me: these are the laws, these the only treaties that remain.' So he, looking hostile at his brother; for he burns in his deep heart, that countless comrades, that a royal helmet, and a steed spread with purple, that a shield gleams tawny with metal, though he himself is not dishonoured in his arms, nor shining with a common cloak: Argia herself had wrought the work in Maeonian fashion, and with skilled thumb had joined golden threads to the purple web.

And now onto the dusty plain, the Furies urging them, they leap forth, and each one's companion goads and warns him. The Furies themselves hold the reins and the trappings, and adorn the gleaming arms with their hand, and increase the plumes with mingled serpents. There stands kindred crime upon the field, the huge war of a single womb, and the matched faces meet beneath the helmet, the standards quail, the trumpets fall silent, and the horns of Mars are stupefied; thrice from the black shores the greedy ruler thundered, and thrice shook the depths of the soil, and the very gods of arms fled: nowhere is glorious Virtue, Bellona quenched her torches, and from afar the trembling Mars snatched away his car, and the maiden warrior, grim with the Gorgon, withdrew, and in their stead the Stygian sisters came. The wretched crowd juts from the lofty roofs, all is wet with tears and from every citadel comes lamentation. Here the old men grieve to have lived, here with bare breast the mothers stand and forbid their little sons to watch, the Tartarean ruler himself even bids the Ogygian shades go forth through the unbarred gate to the kindred monstrosity. They settle upon their native mountains and with a mournful ring stain the day and rejoice that their crimes are surpassed.

When Adrastus heard that they were going to the contest with open goads, and that no shame now stood against the crime, he flies up and flings his reins into their midst, he indeed both great in his realms and venerable in age. But what among such men, to whom not even their own pledges are a care, is an outsider's honour? Yet he begs: 'Shall we then watch this crime, sons of Inachus and Tyrians? Where are the laws and the gods, where is war? Do not persist in your purpose, I entreat you, enemy — though, did this wrath allow it, you too are not far from me in blood — you, son-in-law, I both entreat and command; if so great is your longing for the sceptre, I lay aside the royal garb, go, possess Lerna and Argos alone!' No words of greater persuasion break the kindled men, nor stand against their efforts once undertaken, than the Scythian Pontus, rising with curved waves, ever forbade the Cyanean mountains to clash together, when he sees that his prayers have perished, and the horn-hoofed steeds poured to battle in twofold dust, and the thongs of the raging men tested upon their fingers, he flees, leaving all, the camp, the men, his son-in-law, Thebes, and drives Arion, turned against the yoke, as he warns of the fates: as, let down from his car after the prizes of the leftward lot, the guardian of the shades and the last heir of the world grew pale, coming into Tartarus when heaven was lost.

Yet Fortune did not indulge the fight, and delaying at the first crime, she halted and tarried a little. Twice the ways perished, vain; twice a kindly straying turned aside the horses driven hand to hand, and the spears, pure of the unspeakable blood, fell with slanting strokes, they tighten the reins with their hands, they press with savage spurs the undeserving steeds; and the venerable portent of the gods moves the twin squadrons, and they roll alternate murmurs, muttering: often the impulse is to renew the lines, to run forth and to set the whole war against the wretched pair.

Long since, offended by the lands and the assembly of the gods, Piety sat in a part of heaven turned away, not in the garb in which she was known before, not with serene face, but with her hair stripped of fillets, and the fraternal war, as an unhappy sister of the fighters or an anxious mother, she bewailed, and crying out against savage Jove and the guilty Fates, and that, the poles and the light abandoned, she would go down to Erebus and now preferred the Stygian household: 'Why,' she said, 'O Nature, leader of all, did you create me, to stand against the savage minds of living things and often of the gods? Nothing now have I among the peoples, nowhere is reverence for us, O fury, O men, and the dread arts of Prometheus! How well, after Pyrrha, the earth and the sea lay empty! Behold the mortal race!' she said, and watching her time, 'Let us try help,' she said, 'though I attempt it in vain.' And she leaped down from the pole, a snowy track beneath the black clouds, though mournful, follows the goddess' footsteps, scarcely had she stood upon the field, when the ranks began to grow gentle with sudden peace and to feel the crime; then their faces grow wet and their breasts, and a silent dread crept upon the brothers, wearing too feigned arms and a man's attire, 'Come on, go, resist, now these, now those,' she cries, 'who has sons and brothers at home, who has so great pledges . . . here too — is it not plain that the gods of their own accord pity? — their weapons fall, the horses falter, Chance itself resists.' She had somewhat moved the wavering pair, had not grim Tisiphone marked the deceits, and, swifter than heavenly fire, been there, upbraiding: 'Why do you set yourself against the daring of war, sluggish power, given over to peace? Yield, shameless one: ours is this field and ours the day; now too late you defend the guilty Thebes. Where were you then, when Bacchus stirred the wars and the orgies maddened the armed mothers? Or where were you sluggish, while the serpent of Mars drank the impious pools, while Cadmus ploughed, while the conquered Sphinx fell, while the father begged Oedipus, while by our torch Jocasta came into the chamber?' So she presses on, and, besides, upon her, shrinking from the sight even and drawing her modest face far back, she bears down with hissing snakes and threatens with torches; the goddess draws the cloak cast down over her eyes, and flees, to complain to the great Thunderer.

Then indeed their wraths were kindled with greater goads: arms please them, and the turned cohorts wish to watch, they renew the cruel crime; the impious king fits his weapon and first seizes the chance of the deadly spear. It, attempting a way through the middle orb of the shield, does not carry through the stroke and is mastered by the deep gold. Then the exile comes on and aloud prays his deadly prayer: 'Gods, whom Oedipus, his face gouged out, not in vain besought to set fire to crime, I ask no shameless vows: I will atone with my hands and cut open my own breast with the same iron, if only this man, dying, leave me holding the sceptre, and the lesser shade carry this grief with him.' The swift spear comes between the rider's thigh and the horse's flank, willing death to both; but the blow, the seated man's knee being slackened, was avoided; yet the spear-point, cheated of its vow, finds wounds in the slanting ribs. The steed rushes headlong, scorner of the tightened rein, and writes the reddening fields with a bloody circle. The exile exults, believing this his brother's gore: and he himself believes it through fear; and now the exile gives full rein to his haste, and blindly drives his eager course upon the wounded horse, the reins and hands and weapons are confounded, and with their steps thrown into confusion both plunge to the ground, as ships by night, which the cloudy south wind has entangled, break their oars and exchange their ropes, and after long struggling with the darkness and the storm and themselves, just as they were, sink together into the lowest deep: such is the face of the fight, they meet without order, without art, only with passion and wrath, and they discern the kindling hatreds through their helmets, and search out each other's faces with a bitter eye: no middle ground of earth, and their swords are entangled and their hands interlocked, and the alternating savage murmurs they catch as if they were war-trumpets or the signals of clarions. As when headlong wrath has driven, hand to hand, the lightning boars and raised their bristles in stiffened hair: their eyes tremble with fire, and their crescent jaws with the curved tusks ring; the hunter watches the fights from a near rock, patient, and counsels silence to his dogs: so greedily they rush together; not yet do they mingle deadly wounds, but the blood is begun, and the crime is done. Nor now is there need of the Furies; they only marvel and stand by, praising, and grieve that the frenzies of men can do more than theirs. Each, raging, longs for and aims at his brother's gore, and knows not that his own flows; at last the exile rushes in, and urging on his hand, whose wrath was stronger and crime more just, drove the sword deep into his brother's body, where the breastplate, badly now with its feathers, covers the lowest groin, he, not yet grieving, but terrified by the first chill of the iron, gathers his confused limbs behind his shield; soon, the wound understood, more and more sickly he pants, nor does he spare his retreating foe and rebukes him: 'Whither do you draw back your steps, brother? This is the rest weakened with sleep, this worn out by kingship, this the long rule beneath the shade! Limbs trained by exile and by needy fortunes you see; learn to bear arms, and not to trust in prosperity.'

So the wretched pair fight; there remained to the accursed leader a weary life and the last blood, and for a little while his steps could stand; but of his own will he falls, and prepares his last deceit in the midst now of death, the shout lifts up Cithaeron, and the brother, thinking he had conquered, raised his palms to heaven: 'It is well! I have not vowed in vain, I see the heavy eyes and the face swimming in death. Hither, someone, quickly, the sceptre and the ornament of his hair, while he sees.' Saying this, he moved his steps and his arms, as if about to bear the glory to the temples and to his exulting country, he longs even to despoil the arms; not yet with his hands' work done, that man kept his soul for avenging wraths. And when he felt the other standing over and bent above his breast, he secretly raises his sword and with hatred filled out the thin remnants of his failing life, and the sword, now glad of his fate, he left in his brother's heart. But that one: 'Are you alive, or does anger still survive, treacherous one, never to deserve the seats of rest? Hither with me to the shades! There too I shall demand the compact again, if only the Cnossian urn of the Agenorean judge stands, where it is given to punish kings.' Speaking no more he fell, and heavy with all his arms crushed his brother.

Go, savage souls, and pollute with your death the deadly Tartarus, and exhaust all the punishments of Erebus! And you, Stygian goddesses, now spare the woes of men: in all the lands and under every age let one day have seen this crime, and let the infamous prodigy fall out of mind for those to come, and let kings alone remember these battles.

But the father, the end of the crime discovered, burst forth from the deep darkness, and on the savage threshold brings out his imperfect death: each of his grey locks stands foul with old gore, and his hair, hard with blood, veils his frantic head; far within, his face and cheeks and the traces of his gouged-out light are squalid. The maiden meanwhile sustains the weight of his imposed left hand, his right rests on a staff, as if, his ship abandoned, the loathing ploughman of sluggish Avernus, hating the shades, should go forth to the upper world and trouble the sun and the pale stars, nor himself for long brave and patient of the upper air; meanwhile, the master long lacking, the work would grow greater, and the ages would wait upon all the banks: so he enters the field, and to his companion, lamenting his end, 'Lead me,' he says, 'to my sons and to their father, I pray, and cast me upon the fresh corpses!' The maiden delays, not knowing what he intends; arms, men, cars block the way and delay him, entangled, and amid the high carnage the old man's steps fail, and the pitiable guide labours, when the cry of the maiden showed the long-sought bodies, she lays him over all the cold limbs. Nor is there any voice for the old man: he lies and bellows over the bloody wounds, nor do the words long attempted follow, while he handles the helmets and seeks the hidden faces, at last the father, long mute, loosens his sighs:

'Do you, piety, slow, strike my mind after a long while? Is there beneath this heart any human gentleness? You conquer, O Nature, you conquer the wretched parent! Lo, I have groans, and tears creep along the dry wounds, and the impious hand follows into the soft beating of the breast, receive the due funeral rites of an unspeakable death, cruel ones, and too much mine! Nor is it allowed to know my sons and to fit my address to them; tell me, maiden, your suppliant, whom do I hold? With what honour now, savage as I am, shall I attend your funeral rites? O if my eyes, to be gouged again, would come back, and the power to rage upon faces in my wonted way! Alas the grief, alas the parent's prayers heard more than was just, and the evil entreaties! Who was that god who stood beside me as I prayed, and dictated to the Fates the words snatched too soon? That frenzy moved, and the Erinys, and the father, and the mother, and the kingdom, and the falling eyes; I in nothing: by Dis I swear and the sweet darkness and my innocent guide, so may I go down to Tartarus by a worthy death, nor let Laius flee me, an angry shade, ah me, what knots of brothers, what wounds I handle! Loosen, I pray, their hands, and at last part the hostile bonds, and now at least admit their father between them.' Having so lamented, little by little he had taken on the wraths of death, and was secretly seeking a weapon, did not his daughter forbid it; but Antigone with cautious hand had withdrawn the swords, the old man then rages: 'Where are the guilty weapons? Alas, Furies! Has all the iron gone into their bodies?' As he speaks, his weary companion lifts him and presses down her own dumb grief, glad to have bewailed her savage parent.

But long since, terrified by the clamour of the begun fight, the queen had brought from the inner chambers the well-known sword, the sword, the lamentable spoil of sceptre-bearing Laius. And having complained much to the gods and of her dreadful couch and of her son's furies and of her first husband's shade, she struggled with her right hand, and into her downturned breast scarcely the iron entered at last: the wound bursts through her aged veins, and the unhappy bed is hallowed with blood, collapsing over her, Ismene dried the stroke hissing in her slight breast with her tears and her hair, beating her breast: as in the Marathonian wood tearful Erigone, near the funeral of her slain father, her complaints spent, had now begun to loose the grim knot and, about to die, was binding the strong branches.

And now the glad hope of the two leaders that they had cheated the Amphionian state, and grudging Fortune had transferred the sceptre to another hand, and Creon held the laws of Cadmus. Wretched, alas, the end of the wars! For them the brothers had fought, and him both the Mavortian seed proclaim, and Menoeceus, given a little before for his country, reconciles to the peoples, and he climbs the throne of Aonia, fatal to tyrants, lamentable: ah, coaxing power and ill-counselling love of the sceptre! Will the examples of the former never cleave to the new? See, it pleases him to stand in the accursed place and to handle in his hand the bloody covering! What can you do, better Fortune? Now he begins to bend his father and to blot out Menoeceus with the kingdom given him. First, indeed, steeped in the savage ways of the court, as a sign and a sample of himself, he bids the Danaans be kept from the final fire, and left beneath the bare sky, the unhappy war and the sad shades without resting-places, soon, meeting at the threshold of the Ogygian gate Oedipus returning, he feared him a little, and confessing himself the lesser in silence, checked his ready anger; but he turns again to the king and, more boldly upbraiding the blind foe from afar, 'Go,' he says, 'an omen hateful to the victors, and turn away the Furies and purge the Theban walls by your departure! Your long hope is fulfilled: go, your sons lie dead. What vows now remain to you?' He shuddered at the rabid prompting, and his cheeks stood trembling as if at the sight of their squalor, and his old age withdrew, then he let his daughter and his staff fall from his hand, and, leaning on his wrath, breaks his voice from his swelling breast:

'Is there now leisure to rage, Creon? Just now, pitiable one, you have come into the treacherous kingdom and the place of our fortune, and is it now lawful for you to trample on the ruins of kings? Do you already bar the conquered from tombs, your allies from the walls? Bravo, you can worthily guard the sceptre of Thebes. This is your first day, but why, mad one, do you make new laws contrary? Why do you measure so great honours narrowly? You threaten exile. The timid harshness of kings is that! Why not greedily steep your savage swords at once? Believe me, you may; let a satellite come, eager to obey, and undismayed cut a neck that does not avoid him. Begin! Or do you wait until, bent low with suppliant hand, I be laid prostrate and seek the footsteps of a cruel master? But suppose you try, will you allow it? Do you threaten me any punishment, or think any fears remain? Do you bid me leave my dwelling? Heaven and earth I left of my own accord, and, cruel, turned my avenging hand back upon my face with none compelling me: what such thing can you bid me, hostile king? I flee and depart from the accursed seats; or does it matter where I carry my long funeral and my darkness? Let not every nation grant my prayer, how much of my country's earth, wretched, do I lie upon? But sweet Thebes! Of course here my origin is brighter, and better stars caress my face, here my mother and my sons; have and rule the Theban walls, with the omen under which Cadmus, under which Laius reigned, and I as well; so may you take your marriage chamber, so your faithful pledges, nor let it be your valour to escape fortune with your hand, but, caught, may you love the light. Enough have I sanctioned omens, lead, come, my daughter, far away; but why do I add you to my griefs? Give me, great king, a guide.' The pitiable Antigone feared to be left, and changes her prayers: 'By your happy kingdom, venerable Creon, and by the sacred shade of Menoeceus: grant pardon to the afflicted and forgive his proud words. This manner of speaking his long laments have made; nor is that fierce one so to you alone: thus he addresses the fates and the gods, hard in his grief, and gentle not even to me often; long since in his untamed breast there lives a wretched freedom and the harsh hope of a savage death. And now, lo, cunningly he provokes your wraths and longs for punishment; but you, I pray, may you possess the greater goods of empire, and, lofty, pass over the fallen, and reverence the great funerals of the former leaders, and he too, once exalted on the throne and fenced with arms, gave help to the wretched and justice, equal to the powerful and the suppliant; he who now, out of so great a host, has one companion, and was not yet an exile. Does this man stand against the fortunate? Against him do you go forth with hatred and the strength of the kingdom, drive him from your roofs? Or is it lest near the threshold, illustrious, he should groan and stray, untimely, among your vows? Lay aside your fear: removed far off from your court, he shall weep; I will subdue the upright one and teach him to serve, I will lead him from the assemblies and hide him in a lonely seat. He will be an exile. For what foreign walls will open to him as he migrates? Do you wish him to go to Argos and creep, squalid, into hostile Mycenae, and at the threshold of conquered Adrastus report the Aonian disasters, and the Theban king beg for slight help? What pleasure to spread open the crimes of a wretched race, what to display its shameful misfortunes? Hide, I pray, whatever we are, nor do we beg long gifts, Creon: pity the old man, and his mournful parent's shades here, I pray, here grant me to lay: surely it is allowed to bury Thebans.' So she prays and rolls upon the ground; her father leads her away and savagely threatens, indignant, the pardon, as a lion beneath a high rock, whom once, in his green prime, the woods and mountains trembled at, now sluggish and disarmed by long age, lies, yet his face is great and his old age not to be approached; and if a bellowing should come to his sunken ears, he rears and remembers himself, and groans at his loosened strength and that other lions reign in the fields.

Creon is bent by the speech, but yet the ruler does not grant all to the suppliant's tears, and cuts off part of the gift. 'You shall not,' he says, 'be kept far from your father's borders, so long as by your coming you do not defile the pious temples and homes. Let the haunts hold you, and your Cithaeron; and lo, this land is habitable for your shades, where the war and the twin races lie in blood.' So he speaks, and with the feigned assent of his companions and the groaning crowd, swelling, made for the royal threshold.

Meanwhile the routed Pelasgians abandon by stealth the deadly rampart; none has his own standards or his own leader: they go silent everywhere, and for a fair death embracing a dishonourable life and a shameful return. Night favours them and embraces the fugitives with welcome shadow.

Not yet had the watchful sunrise tilted all the stars in the pole, and the Moon with thinner horn was watching the day press on, when now the Tithonian goddess scatters the timorous clouds and prepares the great heaven for returning Phoebus: already the Dircaean bands stray through their scattered homes, complaining of the delays of night; though then at last there was leisure and the first sleep after the wars, yet sickly peace puts flight to rest, and victory remembers the savage war, scarcely do they dare at first to step forth and loosen the defences of the rampart, scarcely with courage to unbar all the gates; their old fears stand before their eyes, and the dread of the empty plain: as when the earth, tossed by a ceaseless sea, seems at first to reel, so, astonished, they marvel that nothing comes against them, and think the scattered squadrons are rising, so when, scaling the threshold of a clear-seen tower, the Idalian birds have spied the tawny serpent, they drive their young within and wall the brooded nests with their claws and rouse their unwarlike wings to battle; soon though he rush back, yet the white throng fears the bare air, and at last, having begun their flight, shudders and even from the mid stars still looks back.

They go among the bloodless people and the remnants of the prostrate war, wherever grief and bloody mourning have driven the leaders; these see the weapons, these the bodies, but those only the faces of the slain and the breasts of others beside them; some bewail the cars and speak to the widowed horses, because this alone is left; some press kisses on the great wounds and complain of their courage. The cold carnage is sorted out: hands lay open, severed with their hilts and spears, and arrows standing fixed in the midst of eyes; for many there are no traces of the slaughter, they rush in, their lament hovering and everywhere ready, but around the shapeless trunks a pitiable contest rises, who shall bring the rites, who lead the funerals. Often even, deceived — Fortune sported a little while — they wept over enemy men; nor is there sure power to know what blood the wretched should avoid or trample, but those whose house is unharmed and free of grief either range the deserted tents of the wandering Danaans and fling in their torches, or — what chance there is after the war — they search in what dust scattered Tydeus lies, whether the cave of the snatched augur lies open, or where the foe of the gods is, whether ethereal embers still live among his limbs. Now the day is spent with tears, nor did the late evening drive them off: the wretched love laments and feast upon their woes. Nor did they go beneath their roofs, but round the corpses all night the throng sits, and by turns, groaning in alternation, they drive off the beasts with fire and beating of breasts; nor, conquered by the sweet stars, nor with ceaseless weeping did their eyes close, the third Lucifer fought against the Dawn, and now, the mountains bereaved, the glory of the groves, the great beams of Teumesos came, and Cithaeron, friend to the pyres with its wood; the entrails of the cut-down race burn on the heaped-up piles: the Ogygian shades rejoice in the last gift; the naked cohort of the Greeks complains, pitiable, and groaning circles round the forbidden fire, the savage shade of Eteocles too receives unjust honours, by no means royal; the Argive brother is bidden to be held still, and an exile is driven from the flame.

But the king his father and Thebes do not permit Menoeceus to smoke on a common pyre, nor did they build a cheap pyre of oak in the wonted way; but a warlike mound is heaped with cars and shields and all the arms of the Greeks; above the hostile heaps he himself, as victor, his hair adorned with peace-bearing laurel and fillets, reclines: no otherwise than when, the stars demanding it, the Tirynthian lay, glad, on kindled Oeta. Upon the living funeral-offerings the father slaughtered the captive bodies of the Pelasgians and the bridled horses, the solaces of war to the brave man; with these the lofty fire throbs, and at last the paternal groans burst forth:

'O if too great an ardour for great-souled praise had not seized you, my son, venerable with me in the Echionian household and meant to rule beyond me, you who now make bitter the coming joys and the thankless gift of the kingdom! You, though you dwell in the vaults of the gods above and their company with eternal valour — so indeed I believe — to me forever a god to be wept will you be: let Thebes raise altars and lofty temples to you; let it be right for one father to mourn, and now, alas, what worthy rites or what funeral can I bestow on you? Not if I had power to mix fatal Argos and Mycenae, driven against it, into ashes, and myself upon them, I whose life — abomination! — and honour are won by my son's blood; did the same day, the same impious war send you, my boy, and your dread brothers wretchedly into Tartarus? And now is the fortune of grief for Oedipus equal to mine? How like, good Jupiter, are the shades we bewail! Receive, my son, the fresh offerings of your triumph, receive also this guidance of my right hand and the bonds of my proud brow, which you gave your father with little cause for gladness. A king, you a king, let the sad shades of Eteocles behold.' Saying this, he tears at his hair and his hand, and, his anger kindled, more violently he repeats:

'Come then, let them call me savage and harsh, if I forbid the dead of Lerna to burn with you; would it were right to add long feeling to the bodies, and to drive the guilty souls from heaven and Erebus, and to follow the very beasts, the very curved beaks of the birds, and to point out the unspeakable limbs of the kings! Ah me, that the kindly earth and the day will dissolve them where they lie. Wherefore again and again I declare it: let no one dare to help the Pelasgians with last aid and with flames; or, if he does, he shall pay with his death and fill out the number of the bodies taken; by the gods and by great Menoeceus I swear.' He spoke, and his companions, taking him up, bore him into the dwelling.

Meanwhile, escorted, in tears, from empty Argos — rumour draws the wretched ones on — bereaved and widowed the women of Inachus rushed forth like a captive band; each has her own wounds, all have the same garb, hair cast down upon the breast and girdled bosoms; their torn faces stream with bloody nails, and their soft arms grow rough with beating. First through the stunned bands of the black throng the queen, sinking among the sorrowing families and rising again, seeks the way, helpless, Argia; not the palace is in her heart, not her father: one faith, one name, of her beloved Polynices, sits upon her lips; Dirce and the ill-omened walls of Cadmus she would choose to dwell in, Mycenae set aside. Next, drawing the Calydonian women mingled with the Lernaean band to Tydeus' funeral, not yielding to her sister, comes Deipyle; she indeed had heard the crime and the profane biting of her husband, pitiable; but to him lying low all things unhappy love forgives. After her, harsh to behold, and yet to be wept, Nealce, summoning Hippomedon with worthy lament, then the augur's impious wife, alas, about to set up empty pyres. The last of the mourning bands the bereaved companion of Maenalian Diana leads, and grievous Evadne: this one grieves and complains of the toils of her bold boy, that one, mindful of her great husband, goes weeping grimly and is angry at the highest stars. And Hecate, watching them from the Lycaean groves, follows them with her groans, and the Theban mother bewailed them from her Isthmian tomb as they went to the double shore, and Eleusis, though she mourns for herself, wept for the night-wandering band and brought out for the wanderers her secret fires, Saturnia herself leads them by hidden paths and conceals the ways, lest the people of their own, having met them, forbid them to go, and the glory of the great enterprise perish, and Iris too has the care of tending the dead bodies of the leaders, and bedews their rotting limbs with secret dews and the juices of ambrosia, that they may resist longer and await the pyre and not crumble before their time.

Lo, squalid in his cheeks and pale with an empty wound, Ornytus — here deserted by the band of his comrades, a fresh blow slows him — by timid stealth through secret byways takes his feeble road and leans upon a broken spear, and when he was amazed at the lonely places stirred by a new tumult and the band of women, whom now above the bands of Lerna he alone sees, he does not ask the way or the reasons, for they are plain, but with sad face he thus first forestalls them:

'Whither, wretched ones, whither do you bear your way? Do you hope for a funeral and ashes for your slain men? There stands, ever wakeful, a guardian of the shades, and the unburied bodies he reckons up to the king. Nowhere are tears, the approach of men is driven far off: to the birds and beasts alone is it allowed to go; will Creon, fair, grant honour to your mourning? Sooner may you win over the altars of pitiless Busiris and the hunger of the Odrysian stall and the Sicilian gods; he will snatch you, perhaps, as you pray, if his mind is known to me, and over your nuptial funerals he will not slay you, but far from the dear shades. Why do you not flee, while the road is safe, and, returned to Lerna, give what is left, the names, bereaved, to empty tombs, and call the absent souls to vacant pyres? Or do you implore the Cecropian help — for nearby, and the report is that Theseus returns glad from his Thermodontian triumph? Creon must be forced by war and arms into civilized ways and into man.' So he spoke, but for them their tears froze, and the immense impulse of their going was stunned, and their faces were chilled with one pallor. No otherwise, if ever the fasting murmur of a Hyrcanian tigress breathes upon the soft heifers, and the very field is troubled at the sound, a vast fear comes upon all, which one she will choose, on whose shoulders that hunger will climb.

At once their discordant opinion, with various movement, is split: to these it pleases to go round to Thebes and swollen Creon, to these, if the clemency of the Actaean race grant anything; the last of cares and shameful is to return. Here Argia gathers the sudden love of a valour not womanly, and, monstrously laying aside her sex, handles the work: it pleases her — the hard hope of a noble danger! — to approach hand to hand the laws of the unspeakable kingdom, where no daughter of Rhodope nor nursling of snowy Phasis would go, fenced with unwed cohorts. Then she contrives a trick by art, by which she may part herself from her faithful band, and, scorner of her life and reckless with her great grief, may provoke the pitiless gods and the bloody king; piety urges her on, and chaste fires. He himself too is plain before her eyes in every act, now a guest of the wretched woman, now a bridegroom at the first altars, now a gentle husband, now beneath his grim helmet sorrowful in her embrace, and from the topmost threshold often looking back: but no image turns more frequently in her mind than that which, from the blood of the Aonian field, comes naked and demands the pyre. With these furies, anxious in mind, she sickens, and, with the chastest passion, loves the dead man: then, turned to her Pelasgian companions:

'You,' she says, 'make for the Actaean lines and the Marathonian arms, and may Fortune favour the pious labour: let me alone, who was the only cause of so great a ruin, enter the Ogygian homes and bear the first bolts of the kingdom; nor in vain shall we beat upon the deaf thresholds of the savage city: there I have a father-in-law and I have sisters of my husband, and I shall go up to Thebes not unknown. Only do not call back my steps: thither my great impulse and the augury of my mind.' No more, and Menoetes alone — once the guardian and counsellor of her maiden modesty — she chooses, and, though untrained and ignorant of the places, takes her headlong steps the way Ornytus had come. And when she seemed to have left her companions in woe far off, 'Shall I,' she says, 'while you decay through the hostile fields — ah grief! — wait, what the resolve of slow Theseus may be? Whether the chiefs assent to war, whether the soothsayer is favourable? Meanwhile the corpse dwindles. And do we not rather set these limbs beneath the curved birds? And now you complain of me as hard, if any sense remains to you among the shades, of me as slow to the Stygian gods, most faithful one. Alas if still naked, alas if now perhaps buried: each is our crime; is there then no power to the grieving, no Death anywhere, nor savage Creon? You urge me on as I go, Ornytus!' So saying, with great pace headlong she seizes the Megarian fields, each one she meets points out the nearest way and shudders at her aspect and stands in awe of the wretched woman. She goes fierce in look, fearing nothing in heart or ear, and trusting in her too-great woes, and nearer to being feared: as when, lamented through the Phrygian night, Dindyma re-echoes, the maddened leader of the chorus is borne to the stream of pine-bearing Simois, whom the goddess, his blood chosen, herself gave the iron and marked with the filleted bough.

Now father Titan had hidden his car, blazing in the Hesperian flood, to return from other waves, yet she, her heavy toil beguiled by grief, knows not that the day has gone: nor would she be borne through the darkening fields, nor does she break her way through pathless rocks and beams about to slip and the secret places of the woods, black on a clear day, and the new fields cut by hidden ditches, heedless of the ford through the rivers, and past the slumbers of beasts and the dread lairs haunted by monsters, so much do courage and grief avail! It shames Menoetes to go more slowly, and he marvels at the pace of his weak ward, what homes of beasts and men did she not strike with her grievous groaning! How often, as she went, the path was lost, and the solaces of the friendly flame deserted her wandering and the cold darkness overcame her torch! And now the slopes of Pentheus' ridge bend back, wearied, and gape wide far around, when, with panting breast, now nearly failing, Menoetes thus begins his words:

'Not far off, if the hope of my finished labour does not flatter, Argia, I think the Ogygian homes lie, and the pyres that lack a tomb; close at hand the foul air seethes heavy, and the great birds return through the void, this is that cruel ground, nor are the walls far. Do you see how the plain spreads out the huge shadows of the walls, and how the dying fire flickers from the watchtowers? The walls are near; just now the night itself was more silent, and the stars alone loosened the blackening darkness.' Argia shuddered, and stretching her right hand toward the walls: 'City longed for before, now hostile dwellings, Thebes, and yet, if you give back unharmed the shade of my husband, so too you are sweet soil; do you see in what attire I am dressed, with what escort attended, that close to your thresholds first I come, the daughter-in-law of great Oedipus? My vows are not shameless: as a guest I ask the pyre and the lament and the funeral, him, I pray, the exile from the kingdom and routed by war, him, whom you did not deem worthy of his father's throne, give him back to me! And you, I pray, come, if any image exists for the shades and souls wander, freed after the limbs, do you unfold the ways for me, and lead me yourself to your funeral, if I have deserved it!' She spoke, and reaching the shepherd's roof of a nearby hut, restores the breath of the spent fire, and bursts in tumult upon the dreadful fields, as, her torch kindled from the Aetnaean rocks, bereaved Ceres lit up with the changing image of the great flame the Ausonian and Sicilian shore, gathering in the dust the traces of the dark ravisher and the vast furrows; at her frenzied howls Enceladus himself bellows back and lights the ways with bursting fire: the rivers, woods, seas, clouds cry Persephone, only the hall of her Stygian husband is silent of Persephone.

Her faithful guardian warns her, astonished, to remember Creon and to lower her torch in secret stealth, the queen, lately dreaded through the Argive cities, the immense vow of suitors and the most august hope of her race, beneath the hostile night, with no leader and the foe near, alone through the obstacles of arms and the grass slippery with gore, not the darkness, not the encompassing assemblies of shades trembling at, nor the souls bewailing their own limbs, often with blind step she dissembles the iron and the trampled weapons, and her only toil is to have avoided the fallen, while she thinks every corpse her own, and with keen gaze searches out those laid there and turns the prone bodies face up, leaning over, and complains that the stars give too little light.

By chance, through the sleep-bringing shadows of the secret sky, Juno, having stolen herself from the bosom of her great husband, was going to the walls of Theseus, to bend Pallas and open easy Athens to the pious suppliants, and when from the height of the sky she looked back and saw guiltless Argia weary with vain straying through the fields, she grieved at the sight, and meeting the lunar pair turned her face and thus spoke with gentle voice:

'Grant me a small gift as I ask, Cynthia, if any honour for Juno remains; surely at the wicked bidding of Jove you thrice prolonged the Herculean night — but I let go old complaints: lo, here is a chance for service: the most pleasing worshipper of mine, Inachian Argia, do you see by what night she strays, nor can the sick woman find her husband in the dense darkness? And for you too the cloudy radiance grows faint: thrust forth, I pray, your horns, and let your orbit press nearer the earth than is its wont, this one too, who bends the dripping reins for you in your car, let down upon the Aonian watchmen, Sleep.' Scarcely had she said it, when, the clouds rent, the goddess brought forth her great orb; the shades took fright, and the gleam was cut back from the stars; Saturnia herself scarcely bore the flames.

First, through the fields, by the in-poured light, the pitiable woman herself recognizes her own labours by the cloak of her husband, though the weaving is hidden and the purple mourns, suffused with blood; and while she calls the gods and thinks this remains of her dear funeral, she sees the man himself in the dust, almost trampled. Her spirit fled, and her sight and her voice, and grief shut in her tears; then with her whole body she stretches over his face and seeks through kisses the absent soul, and gathers the blood pressed in his hair and garment, to keep it, soon at last, her voice returning:

'Is it you, my husband, set out for your due kingdom, the leader of the war and son-in-law of powerful Adrastus, whom I behold, and is it such triumphs of yours that I meet? Lift hither your cheeks and your failing eyes: there comes to your Thebes Argia; come, lead me into the walls and show your ancestral home and return the mutual hospitality, alas, what do I do? Cast out on the bare turf, this much of your native land you have, what quarrels? Surely your brother does not hold the empire; have you stirred no tears of your own? Where is your mother, where is glorious Antigone of the famous report? For me indeed you lie, for me alone you are conquered! I used to say: whither do you direct your road? Why do you demand the denied sceptre? You have Argos, you will reign in your father-in-law's hall; here is lasting honour for you, here undivided power. Why do I complain? I myself gave the war and sadly begged my father myself, that I might now hold you, such as this, embraced, but it is well, you gods, I am grateful, Fortune; the distant hope of the journey is accomplished: I have found his whole body, ah me, but with how deep a gap the wound descends! Did the brother do this? In what part, I pray, lies that unspeakable plunderer? I shall conquer the birds — let there be power to approach — and shut out the beasts; or does the deadly man have fires too? But neither shall your own land see you destitute of flames: you shall burn and shall have the tears which it is denied to kings to have, and forever, serving your tomb, my deserted faith shall endure, and there shall be a son of grief, and with little Polynices I shall warm the bed.'

Lo, other groans and another torch to the pyres bore pitiable Antigone, having scarcely won the sought exit through the walls; for at all times the watchmen attend her, and the king himself bids her be held, the watches drawn closer and the fire keeping more frequent guard, therefore to the gods and her brother she excuses her delays, and, frantic, when a little the bristling sentry yielded to sent-down sleep, she bursts from the walls: with such a roar as the maiden lioness' wrath terrifies the fields, whose rage at last is free and her first frenzy without her mother, nor did she long delay, for the savage field, and in what dust her brother was laid, she had known: and against her Menoetes sees Argia going, who has the leisure, and checks the groans of his dear ward, yet when the last sound reached the erect ears of the maiden, and when, beneath the black garb and hair, squalid and her face fouled with thick blood, she saw her by the rays of the stars and by both their torches:

'Whose shade,' she says, 'or who, rash, do you seek in my night?' That one for long said nothing, but over her husband's face she casts, and equally over her own, her veils, seized by sudden fear and a little forgetful of her grief, the more chiding the suspect silences, Antigone persists, pressing both the companion and the woman herself; but both fail and stand fixed in silence, at last Argia unveils her face, and yet, embracing the body, declares:

'If you come to seek anything in this old blood of the wars with me, if you too dread the harsh commands of Creon, I can confide and confess myself to you, if you are wretched — surely I see your tears and laments — join, come, join your faith: I am the royal offspring of Adrastus — ah me, is anyone near? — at the pyre of my dear Polynices, though the kingdoms forbid it.' The Cadmean maiden was amazed and trembled at once, and forestalls her as she speaks: 'Me, then — O ignorant chance! — do you fear, the partner of woes, me? You hold my limbs, you bewail my dead. I yield, hold him, alas, shame! the cowardly piety of a sister! This one first—!' Here, fallen together and in an embrace joined over the very man, they eagerly mingle their tears and their hair, and, sharing the limbs, by turns groaning they return to his face, and in alternation take joy of the dear neck. And while now this one recalls her brother, now that one her husband, and beginning in turn they tell over again Thebes and Argos, Argia more at length remembers their wretched fortunes:

'By the holy bond shared in our secret grief, by the allied shades and the conscious stars I swear: not here his lost honours, though a wandering exile, not his native soil, not the heart of his dear mother, you alone did he desire, speaking nights and days of Antigone; I was the lesser care and easy to be left. You, however, perhaps from the lofty citadel, on high, before the crime, giving the standards to the Greek companies, you saw him, and he looked back at you from the very line of battle, saluted with the sword and the nodding peak of his cone: we were far off, but what god drove you to the last wraths? Were your prayers of no avail? Did he deny you this as you begged?' The causes and the sad fates to recount Antigone had begun; her faithful companion warns them both: 'Come, rather, to your undertaking! Already the stars grow pale, troubled by the near day, carry through your labour, there will be time for tears, you shall weep when the fire is lit.'

Not far off the murmurs showed the banks of Ismenos, where it went, still troubled and discoloured with blood. Hither they carry the torn limbs by their joint effort, the feeble women, and the companion, no stronger, joins his arms. So the sisters washed Hyperion's Phaethon, smoking, in the warm Po; scarcely had he been laid in his tomb, and the weeping woods stood by the rivers. When the gore was cleansed in the shallows and the honour of death returned to his limbs, the wretched women, after their last kisses, seek a fire; but cold and lifeless are the embers in the crumbling hollows round about, and all the pyres are at rest. There still stood, whether by chance the pyre, or by the will of the gods, to which it was given to scorch the savage limbs of Eteocles, or whether Fortune was again preparing the place for portents, or whether the Fury had kept the fires that would dissent, here a thin light still living in the black oak both eager women alike saw, and at once rejoiced, with cause for tears; nor yet had they found whose pyre it was, but whoever it is, they pray that it, gentle and mild, admit a sharer of the last ash and mingle the shades.

Lo, the brothers again: as soon as the devouring fire touched the first limbs, the pyres trembled and the new stranger is driven from the tomb; the flames overflow with divided crest and flash their alternate tips with broken light. As if pale Orcus had set the fires of the Furies clashing, each globe is threatening and each strives to reach further; the very beams too, their weight stirred a little, drew apart, and the terrified maiden cries out:

'We are undone, and have goaded with our hand the wraths of the dead. It was the brother: for what savage approach of a guest's shade would drive him off? Lo, I recognize the fragment of the shield and the half-burned belt, it was the brother! Do you see how the flame recoils and yet rushes together? The wicked hatreds live, they live, nothing was done by the war; wretched ones, thus, while you move arms, Creon, surely, has conquered! Nowhere now are the kingdoms, what is this ardour? For whom do you rage? Calm your threats; and you, an exile everywhere, ever destitute of fairness, now yield: this your bride begs, this your sister, or we shall come savage into the midst of the fires.'

Scarcely had she said it, when a sudden tremor shook the fields and the high roofs, and the gaping of the discordant pyre aided it, and the rest of the watchmen was troubled, for whom sleep itself was vexing with the images of woes: 'It crashes,' one says, surveying all the prospect, a soldier with an armed cordon, the old man alone fears them pressing on; but they themselves, before the pyre and openly, confess they have scorned the commands of savage Creon and their stealth, with a clear lament, careless, since they see that every corpse has been brought. A contest is held over the savage death, and the spirited hope of dying rages: this one claims to have snatched her brother's, this her husband's limbs, and in turn they prove it: 'I the body, I the fires, me piety, me love led on.' It pleases them to demand savage punishments and to thrust their right hands into the chains. Nowhere is that reverence which lately was in their alternating words, you would think it wrath and hatred; so great is the discordant clamour on either side, and they are dragged to the king, who is to judge them.

But far off, with Pallas now favourable, to the Actaean walls Juno, going before, leads the Phoronean mothers, astonished, no less than she herself, and reconciles the groaning throng to the peoples, and adds honour to the Athenians. She herself with her hand hands them the olive boughs and the suppliant fillets, and teaches them to lower their eyes beneath the spread cloak and to hold out the empty urns without hands. All the ages, poured out from the Erechthean households, fill the houses and the ways: whence this swarm and so many wretched women at once? Not yet do they know the causes of the woes, and already they groan. The goddess mingles herself in both councils, teaching everything, from what race they sprang, what funerals they bewail, or what they seek; and besides, with various addresses, the women themselves loudly and everywhere murmur much against the Ogygian laws and untamed Creon. The Getic birds complain no more in their guest-roofs with mangled speech, when they cry out the double marriage-chamber and unjust Tereus.

In the midst of the city there was an altar granted to none of the powerful gods; gentle Clemency set there her seat, and the wretched made it sacred; never without a new suppliant was she, never did she condemn any vow with refusal, all who ask are heard, and it is given to come night and day and to appease her power with complaints alone, a thrifty worship: no incense-flame, no deep blood is received: the altars sweat with tears, and above hang the offerings of the cut hair of the mournful and the garments left behind when their lot was changed. A gentle grove is round about, marked with venerable worship, filleted laurels and the suppliant's tree, the olive.
